Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Card Component

Guidance

How to choose a configuration, what belongs in each slot, and the rules that keep cards consistent across surfaces.

Choosing

Picking a Thumbnail Type #

Thumbnail Type is a statement about what the card is about. Choose by asking what the user needs to recognize first.

UseWhenDon't
DominantThe visual is the content — link previews, media shares, hero announcements. The 16:9 banner leads.Don't use for dense lists; one Dominant card per viewport region is plenty.
Primary (img 128)The image matters but shares billing with metadata — file previews with rich detail lines.Don't pair with a Title Thumbnail unless both identities are truly distinct.
Secondary (img 72)Compact scannable rows where the image is a recognition aid — trending files, recent documents.Don't put text inside the media; 72px is a glance target.
NoneIdentity lives in the Title Thumbnail or the content itself — site cards, people cards, activity digests.Don't fake a banner inside Slot Above Divider; switch to Dominant instead.
Choosing

Emphasis & Density #

Emphasis answers "how loud is this card right now": Default for resting content, Active for the selected/highlighted state (brand-tinted fill, accent stroke), Floating for cards lifted above the canvas — pickers, previews, drag states. Emphasis is a state, not a style choice; the same card moves through emphases as the user interacts.

Density answers "how much room does this surface have": Comfy is the default for primary canvases, Compact removes 24px of vertical air for dashboards and side panels, and Cardless strips the chrome entirely for embedding inside an already-carded parent — a card within a card should never draw two borders.

Cardless exists to prevent double chrome. If the parent surface already provides containment (a sheet, a grouped list, another card), use Cardless and let the parent own the border.
Slots

Slot Do's and Don'ts #

Slots are contracts. These rules keep slotted content from breaking the card's rhythm.

Slot Above Divider is for content that describes the card's subject — file grids, activity feeds, galleries. Keep it self-contained: no interactive elements that compete with the footer actions.
Slot Below Divider is for content that acts on the subject — composers, reaction strips, expandable detail. If the divider is hidden, prefer Slot Above Divider; a below-slot without a divider reads as unanchored.
Detail line icons should always be 16px Fluent regular-weight glyphs from fluenticons.co. Never scale a 24px icon down — optical weight goes muddy.
Never place a second card inside a slot with chrome on. Use a Cardless instance, or the purpose-built File Card tiles from the OD library.
Footer

Footer Rules #

Maximum two labeled buttons plus the trailing utility slot. First button is the primary action and may take the filled treatment; the second stays outlined. Three or more actions means the extras belong behind More Horizontal in the overflow. Button labels are verbs — "Open", "Share", "Follow" — never nouns. Icon-only buttons are reserved for the trailing 24×24 slot.

The footer is the only interactive zone in a Static card. If the whole card is tappable, the footer becomes redundant — pick one interaction model per card.

Card Component

Architecture

The configuration logic — why the Card is three orthogonal axes plus slots, and how the pieces compose without variant explosion.

Model

The Configuration Model #

The Card separates three concerns that would otherwise multiply into hundreds of bespoke components:

Thumbnail Type is the layout axis — it decides the media footprint and therefore the card's internal flow (stacked for Dominant, side-by-side for Primary/Secondary, text-first for None). Emphasis is the state axis — visual loudness, orthogonal to layout. Density is the context axis — how much room the host surface affords, including the degenerate Cardless case where the host owns containment.

Because the axes are orthogonal, 4 × 3 × 3 = 36 combinations are expressible from one component — and exactly one is excluded (None + Floating + Cardless) because a chrome-free, media-free card has no surface left to elevate. The component set publishes 35 variants.

Content never lives on an axis. What the card shows (files, people, activity) is slot payload; how it's arranged (layout, state, context) is axis configuration. Mixing the two is what causes variant explosion in legacy card libraries.
Structure

Figma Anatomy #

The exact layer tree of the published component — the map for translating the Figma structure to code. Purple entries are slots (swap targets that become SLOT properties at compile time). Blue entries are bound text properties. Items marked optional are hidden by default and toggled per instance.

Card (335 × h · 343 in Cardless · padding 12dp Compact / 20dp Comfy) └─ Primary Container ├─ [slot] Leading Media — banner 295×144, img 128, or img 72×72 └─ Secondary Container ├─ Title Block │ ├─ [slot] Title Thumbnail (48×48) — optional │ └─ Text Column │ ├─ [text] Title │ └─ [text] Caption — optional ├─ Detail Lines — optional │ ├─ Detail Line 1 Row │ │ ├─ [slot] ↳Detail Line 1 Icon (16×16) │ │ ├─ [text] Detail 1 │ │ └─ [slot] Custom Slot — optional │ └─ Detail Line 2 Row │ ├─ [slot] Detail Line 2 Icon (16×16) │ ├─ [text] Detail 2 │ └─ [slot] Custom Slot — optional └─ [slot] Slot Above Divider — optional ├─ Divider (311×1) — optional ├─ [slot] Slot Below Divider — optional └─ Card Footer — optional ├─ ActionGroup │ ├─ PrimaryButton → [slot] Slot (16×16 icon) + [text] Label │ └─ SecondaryButton → [slot] Slot (16×16 icon) + [text] Label └─ [slot] Slot (24×24) → OverflowButton
Naming quirks are load-bearing. The leading ↳ on ↳Detail Line 1 Icon and the bare name on Detail Line 2 Icon are verbatim from the library — the compiler matches slots by exact name, so document-accurate names matter more than tidy ones.
Structure

Container Hierarchy #

Two nested containers give the Card its flexibility:

Primary Container owns the 12px padding and the relationship between Leading Media and everything else. When Thumbnail Type changes, only Primary Container's flex direction changes — column for Dominant (banner above), row for Primary/Secondary (media leading). Nothing inside Secondary Container knows or cares.

Secondary Container owns the text stack: Title Block → Detail Lines → Slot Above Divider. Its rhythm (8px gaps, 4px between detail rows) is constant across every variant, which is why a card re-flows perfectly when you flip axes.

The Divider / Slot Below Divider / Card Footer trio sits outside Primary Container, at the card root. That placement is deliberate: the action zone spans the full card width even when the content zone is split by a leading image.

Slots

Why Slots, Not Props #

Eight regions are slots rather than baked-in content. The reasoning:

A property system (INSTANCE_SWAP with preferred values) can only offer content the library anticipated. Slots invert this — the Card guarantees geometry (position, size bounds, spacing participation) and accepts any content. The File Card grids in the People example and the activity feed in the Site example were never designed into the Card; they compose into Slot Above Divider because the slot only enforces width and rhythm.

Slots are also the hidden-by-default mechanism. Slot Above Divider, Slot Below Divider, Custom Slot, Divider, and Footer all ship hidden. A default Card is title + caption + details — everything else is opt-in. This keeps the property panel honest: enabling a region is a visible, intentional act.

Placeholder promotion: every slot ships with a .placeholders library instance (.Slot Placeholder 295×48, .Image Placeholder 295×144, .Title Thumbnail Placeholder 48×48, .Detail Icon Placeholder 16×16). Placeholders render the diagonal-stripe treatment in specs and are swapped out — never resized — by consumers.
Logic

Visibility & Dependency Logic #

Regions toggle independently, but three dependencies are enforced by convention:

RuleLogic
Divider ⇢ below-contentThe Divider only earns its pixel when something exists on both sides — hide it if neither Slot Below Divider nor Card Footer is on.
Footer ⇢ overflowThe trailing 24×24 slot renders whenever the footer does; swap its content rather than hiding it, so footer geometry stays stable.
Detail Lines ⇢ rowsDetail Lines is a single toggle for the two-row block. Single-row cards hide row 2's content, not the block — keeping the 36px reservation avoids reflow on data change.
Pipeline

Compile Mapping #

How the configuration model lands in the Monocore build pipeline:

Slots become SLOT component properties bound via componentPropertyReferences.slotContentId; regions that pair a slot with a visibility toggle (Slot Above/Below Divider) receive both bindings in a single componentPropertyReferences write — two separate writes would overwrite the first key (R27). Footer button icons ride on isExposedInstance (R25), because the Plugin API blocks property references on instance sublayers (R12). Text properties (Title, Caption, Detail 1/2, Label) bind through characters references after style assignment (R2, R5).

The full 14-phase build and gate table lives in the internal Cold Start Pipeline runbook.

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. Accessibility

Accessibility #

  • Both sizes are under a 44dp target. Default is 28dp and Small is 18dp. Interactive badges must have their hit area extended by the host; the visual pill is never the target.
  • Icon-only badges carry no accessible name. Turning Icon only on removes the label and with it everything announceable. Supply a name explicitly on every icon-only instance.
  • Selected state must be announced. Active is a fill change and a font-size change — neither reaches a screen reader. Expose the selected state programmatically.
  • Small type is set solid and clipped. Caption 2 at 11dp on an 11dp line height inside an 18dp box will truncate rather than reflow at large text sizes. Do not put load-bearing information in a Small badge.

Badge Component

Architecture

Why a five-axis set publishes twenty variants instead of seventy-two, what the two slots are responsible for, and where the published values drift.

Model

The Configuration Model #

Five axes are declared; only three of them are genuinely independent.

Badge type and State are one axis wearing two names. Static publishes only N/A; Interactive publishes Rest and Active. There is no Static Rest and no Static Active, so the real axis has three values — Static, Rest, Active — and splitting it in two is what makes the set look sparser than it is.

Icon only and Left image are also coupled: Icon only is published exclusively with Left image = Icon. An icon-only badge showing an avatar is not expressible, which is correct — an avatar with no label is an Avatar component, not a Badge — but it means the two properties are not orthogonal either.

That leaves Size as the only fully independent axis, and even it is incomplete: Active does not publish at Small.

Tappability is carried by foreground colour and nothing else. Static and Interactive Rest are the same pill with the same surface and the same stroke; only the label colour differs. That is the single most important thing to know about this component, and the reason it cannot be the only signal that something is tappable.
Structure

Figma Anatomy #

A single horizontal row inside a pill. Two slots, left to right, and no trailing affordance anywhere in the set. Purple entries are slots, blue are bound text properties.

Badge view83392-62610 · 20 variants
Badge view (Type × State × Size × Left image × Icon only · radius 999) ├─ [slot] Icon — Left image = Avatar or Icon │ ├─ Avatar (16dp Default · 10dp Small · radius 10000) │ └─ Icon (16 box / 12 glyph Default · 10 box / 6.667 glyph Small) └─ Text container (2dp horizontal padding) └─ [text] Label — hidden when Icon only = True Icon only = True └─ [slot] Placeholder (16 box / 12 glyph Default · 12 box / 8 glyph Small Static · 10 box / 6.667 glyph Small Interactive)

Properties & Slots

Two slots and one bound text property. Everything else is a variant.

NameTypeDefaultNotes
Icon (left image)Instance swapAvatarAvatar 16dp or icon 16 box / 12 glyph at Default; 10dp / 10 box at Small. Hidden when Left image = None.
Text containerContainerVisibleHolds the label with 2dp of horizontal padding. Hidden when Icon only = True.
LabelTextLabelSingle line, never wraps; truncates with ellipsis at Default Static.
Trailing icon——Does not exist. Interactive Rest and Static share identical widths at Default, which confirms it.
No wrappers, no nesting. Like Button, the Badge is a single auto-layout row with at most two children. The variant does all the work — which is why twenty variants can cover a five-axis surface without the component itself becoming complicated.
Known issues

Published Debt #

IssueWhereEffect
No Active state at SmallInteractive · SmallA Small badge can be tapped but cannot show that it is selected — four missing variants
Active raises the label from Body 3 to Body 2Interactive · Active · Icon and NoneSelecting a badge changes its text size and reflows the row it sits in
… except with an Avatar, which stays at Body 3Interactive · Active · AvatarThe size jump is inconsistent within a single state
Three surfaces across the setRaisedSecondary, RaisedTertiary, RaisedPrimarySmall uses a lighter grey than Default, and one Rest variant uses a darker one
Active removes the 1dp strokeInteractive · ActiveThe Active badge is 2dp smaller than its Rest counterpart
Small declares both min-height 16 and height 18All Small variantsCompeting declarations; the minimum is dead code
Icon-only Small geometry differs by TypeStatic 12/8 vs Interactive 10/6.667Same size and content, two different glyph boxes
The missing Active at Small is the one to fix first. It is not a cosmetic inconsistency — it is a state a real interface needs and cannot express. Everything else on this list is drift; this one is a hole.

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Messaging

Guidance

Interaction rules that keep Chat Message and Post behaving the same way regardless of which surface renders them.

Behavior

Core Interaction Rules #

BehaviorRule
See moreExpands the message inline, in place, without navigating away or opening a separate view. Appears once body copy passes 4 lines. No separate “read more” screen.
Reactions overflowShow up to 3 reaction types inline, with a person's name attached to the first one; collapse anything beyond that into a single overflow count rather than wrapping the row.
Reply summarySurface reply count and reactions as one consolidated row directly under the message, not as two separate fragments competing for space.
Thread entryDon't add a standalone “Reply in thread” compose row at the end of a thread. Entry into the thread happens through the same row that already holds the emoji and message actions.
Cross-platform

Teams ↔ Engage Alignment #

Recommendations already adopted from the alignment review. Use these when a value needs to be picked for either surface.

AreaRecommendation
Avatar sizingAlign parent avatars at 36px and reply avatars at 24px across both surfaces — don't inherit either product's legacy sizing independently.
Body spacingUse the two-value 8dp / 12dp scale rather than picking a single number per surface.
TypographyReduce the number of distinct type styles a Post can use — a simpler hierarchy reads faster than more visual variation.
Content densityMatch overall information density between Teams and Engage; don't let one surface feel noticeably denser than the other.
IndentationKeep a cardless, indentation-based layout on both surfaces rather than reintroducing card borders per post.
When Teams and Engage disagree and there's no recorded alignment decision, don't guess. Check the Architecture tab's open-questions table first — several of these are intentionally still pending.

Messaging

Architecture

Why Chat Message and Post are documented as one system, and which platform differences are deliberate versus still being decided.

Model

Shared Model, Divergent Shell #

Chat Message and Post are two presentations of the same underlying primitives — Avatar, Header (name + timestamp), Body, Reactions, Reply/Thread summary. What differs is the shell each primitive set sits inside: Chat Message wraps them in a bubble (own-message accent fill, received-message neutral fill, tail-less grouped blocks for consecutive sends); Post wraps them in a cardless, indentation-based row designed for a scrolling feed.

Building both off one shared model is what let the Teams ↔ Engage alignment work converge dozens of small values — avatar size, spacing, reaction count — without having to reconcile two unrelated components.

This shared-model approach is why the alignment review could treat “avatar sizing” and “reactions” as single line items even though they show up in two visually different components — the primitives are the same, only the shell changes.
Open

Open Questions — Pending Confirmation #

Recorded directly from the design team's alignment notes. Don't treat these as resolved — build against the Spec/Guidance values on the other tabs, but flag any of these three if new information changes them.

AreaTeamsEngageStatus
Reply presentationMessage bubbles for repliesFlat, borderless message presentationMay not need to converge — Teams keeping bubbles is an acceptable permanent divergence.
Sending stateBlank loading state followed by a toast confirmationExisting (pre-alignment) sending experiencePending — decide whether Engage adopts Teams' toast pattern or the two stay different.
Unread indicatorsUses “Me”-message-style bar indicators to communicate unread stateStandard unread indicatorsPending — evaluate whether Engage can adopt the Teams indicator pattern.

Color semantics

Guidance

How to use the semantic surface system correctly — behavioral rules, designer workflow, what the system intentionally leaves out, and WCAG AA accessibility notes.

Rules & workflow Accessibility
Rules

Behavioral Rules #

Five rules govern how the system behaves. Each one closes off a class of mistake the design system has historically made: arbitrary elevation steps, ad-hoc semantics per component, and value drift when context changes.

Semantic stability. A semantic role's meaning never changes. Surface/Floating always means "floating temporary UI surface" — only its tonal value shifts between L1 and L2.
Primary means "always extreme," not "always lighter." Unlike Surface/Canvas, which adapts to its container, Surface/Primary always holds the extreme value (pure white in light, pure black in dark) regardless of elevation. On a Base or Raised container it reads as lifted (lighter in dark mode). But inside a dark Overlay (Grey/10), a Primary card goes to Grey/0 — darker than its container, an intentional inversion. Use it for cards and contained regions that must maintain maximum contrast against their surround rather than blending into the elevation hierarchy.
No new elevations. The system has L1 and L2, and only L1 and L2. Floating is its own thing, not L3.
Floating is not elevation. Menus, popovers, tooltips, and reaction pickers use Surface/Floating regardless of whether they appear in an L1 or L2 parent context. They are transient, not canvas-elevated.
Platform-chrome surfaces are exceptions. Surface/Dominant (top) and Surface/Quaternary (bottom tabs) exist outside the canonical L1/L2 system to give the OS room to impose its own materials. Their declared values are fallbacks — actual rendering may be overridden by iOS 26 large-title materials or Android tab-bar blur on supported devices.
Overlay forces L2. Presenting a modal, sheet, or drawer shifts the parent frame from L1 to L2. This means the apparent Dark L1 value collision between Surface/Overlay and Surface/RaisedSecondary (both resolve to Grey/10) is never actually rendered — by the time Surface/Overlay is on screen, the surrounding tokens have already resolved to their L2 values, where RaisedSecondary becomes Grey/14 and the visual separation returns.
A handful of tokens differ between L1 and L2. The rest resolve to the same value across environment levels. The L1/L2 distinction matters most for: Floating, Sunken, Interactive. (Base and RaisedSecondary share a single value across both L1 and L2 — the environment shift no longer applies to them.)
Workflow

How Designers Use It #

The system reduces every surface decision to two choices: pick the role, set the parent's mode. Everything else resolves automatically.

  1. Pick the semantic role that describes intent (Surface/RaisedBase, Surface/Floating, etc.).
  2. Bind the variable to a fill or stroke.
  3. Set the parent frame's mode (Light L1, Light L2, Dark L1, Dark L2).
  4. The variable resolves to the correct tonal value automatically.

When entering an elevated context (sheet, modal, drawer), the parent frame's mode switches from L1 to L2 — every surface inside picks up the L2 tonal values without changing token names.

Scope

What's Intentionally Excluded (for now) #

The canonical Surface system covers neutral surfaces and strokes. State, brand, text, icon, and component-specific tokens live elsewhere by design.

CategoryWhere it livesRationale
State surfaces
Critical, Success, Info, Accent, Disabled		 Legacy Color collection Pending future State/* layer.
Brand surfaces Separate Brand collection Brand expression is owned independently.
Text and Icon roles Legacy Color collection as Text/* and Icon/* Carry over as-is. The only update is an accessibility pass that improves contrast for Text/* and Icon/* across every surface and stroke role in the system.
Component-specific tokens — Never introduced into Monocore Semantic per the rule "do not create component-specific semantics."
Reference

Accessibility — WCAG AA Contrast #

Every Text/* role measured against every opaque Surface/* role, in the two Theme modes (Light and Dark). Targets: 4.5:1 for normal text (AA Normal) and 3:1 for large text (≥18pt regular or ≥14pt bold) and UI components (AA Large).

Method. WCAG 2.x relative-luminance formula. Text/Disabled is intentionally low-contrast and exempt per spec. Text/On Accent is only evaluated against Surface/Accent. Translucent surfaces (Subtle, Glass, Scrim) must be composited over a known canvas before testing — results below assume an opaque host.

Headline: the system mostly passes

The core pairings — Text/Primary and Text/Dominant on every Surface/Canvas, Surface/Primary, Surface/RaisedBase, Surface/Floating, Surface/Overlay, Surface/Sunken, and the Container family — clear AA Normal in every mode. The weak spots cluster in three places: secondary text on raised dark surfaces, brand-blue link text on raised surfaces, and colored semantic text (Danger, Success, Warning).

Surface/Accent is single-purpose. The brand-blue accent surface (#654cf5 light, #8a80ff dark) is only contrast-safe with Text/On Accent (white in light, black in dark). All other text roles fail AA on Accent — including the brand-blue link colors themselves. If you need accent-colored fill and a non-white text label, switch to a Subtle accent surface and standard Primary text.

Pairings that pass AA Large only (3:1) — not AA Normal

These combinations are safe for headings, buttons, badges, icons, and any UI text at 18pt+ regular or 14pt+ bold. Avoid them for body copy.

ModeSurfaceText roleRatio
Light L1Surface/RaisedPrimaryText/Secondary, Text/Hint4.04

System-level watchlist

Text/Danger sits at the threshold everywhere. Light #d92c2c lands between 3.50 and 4.44 on virtually every neutral surface — never quite reaching AA Normal. Use Danger text only for short labels, icons, or large-text contexts. For destructive copy in body text, pair Surface/Danger with Text/Primary (passes AA on the tinted background), not Text/Danger on a neutral surface.
Brand-blue links struggle on raised dark surfaces. Text/Interactive (and Text/Link) at #8a80ff drops to 3.40 on Surface/Floating in Dark L2 and 3.36 on Surface/RaisedPrimary in Dark L1. Inline links inside floating menus and elevated cards should either be set as large-text (button-style) or paired with an underline + bold treatment to satisfy non-color accessibility requirements.
Secondary text on Dark L1 raised surfaces is borderline. Text/Secondary at #8f8f8f on Surface/Floating (3.63), Surface/RaisedBase (3.91), and Surface/RaisedPrimary (3.36) all fail AA Normal. For body-weight metadata or helper copy inside dark floating UI, prefer Text/Primary instead and rely on size or weight for hierarchy.
Surface/Warning + non-warning text fails in Dark L1. The dark warning surface #4d3a0c is too close in luminance to several text colors. If a warning surface needs anything beyond Text/Dominant, Text/Primary, or Text/Warning itself, plan on increased size or weight.

Recommendations

The Token Table above shows two columns of new dark-mode raised values (Surface/Floating at Grey/22–24, RaisedPrimary at Grey/24) sitting closer to the canvas tier than to the IC variants. That is intentional — the IC ("Increased Contrast") modes exist precisely to deliver AA-Normal-grade results when a user needs stronger separation. Three concrete moves:

  1. Promote Text/Primary as the default body text everywhere. Reserve Text/Secondary for ≥14pt or non-body roles (timestamps, captions, helper labels). The current Secondary value is calibrated for legibility on Canvas, not on every raised tier.
  2. Treat Text/Interactive as a large-text or UI-component role. It works for buttons and tappable labels; for inline body links, fall back to Text/Primary with an underline.
  3. Document the IC modes as the AA-Normal-everywhere variants. When a screen has an accessibility-critical context (forms, financial data, settings), authoring against an IC mode guarantees the full text ramp passes 4.5:1 against every surface.
The full matrix. Every Text × Surface ratio is computed in outputs/contrast.py and saved to outputs/contrast_results.json. Re-run to refresh after any token change — the script reads from the snapshotted token values and prints a fail list per mode.

Color semantics

Architecture

Why the system is built this way — the two-axis model (semantic role × environment level), the four modes it produces, the primitives/semantic/extension layering, and the rationale that keeps components stable across themes.

2 axes 4 modes Layered architecture
Concept

Architecture #

A semantic role describes the purpose of a surface and stays stable across all environments and themes. An environment level describes whether a surface sits in the root app or inside an elevated container. The two axes are orthogonal: pick the role for intent, and the parent frame's mode resolves the role to the right tonal value automatically.

Axis 1 — The "what"

Semantic Surface Roles

Stable, purpose-named tokens like Surface/RaisedBase or Surface/Floating. The role never changes regardless of theme or environment.

Axis 2 — The "where"

Environment Levels

L1 is the root application environment. L2 is an elevated canvas — bottom sheets, modals, drawers. The parent frame's mode controls which value the role resolves to.

Reference

The Two Axes #

Axis 1 — Semantic Surface Roles

A semantic role describes the purpose of a surface and stays stable across all environments and themes.

13 canonical surface roles

RolePurpose
Surface/CanvasRoot canvas plane — adapts to its container
Surface/PrimaryHigh-contrast contained surface that always holds the extreme value (pure white in light, pure black in dark) regardless of elevation
Surface/SubtleTransparent subtle grouping and interaction overlays
Surface/SubtleHoverHovered subtle regions
Surface/SubtleSelectedSelected subtle regions (peers with SubtleHover)
Surface/RaisedBaseStandard contained screen surface. Same value as Surface/RaisedSecondary in every mode — use Base when this color appears at the screen level alongside other elements sharing the same background that aren't part of a grouped container list.
Surface/RaisedSecondarySame value as Surface/RaisedBase, reserved for component surfaces — chips, badges, pill-style controls, and other small contained UI.
Surface/RaisedPrimaryStandard raised contained surface — cards, panels, sheets at default elevation
Surface/FloatingFloating temporary UI surfaces (menus, popovers, reaction pickers)
Surface/OverlayBlocking modal and sheet surfaces
Surface/SunkenInset or embedded regions
Surface/InteractiveInteractive selectable containers
Surface/GlassAcrylic and translucent surfaces
Surface/ScrimBackground dimming overlays
Base and RaisedSecondary share a color, not a role. Both resolve to the same value in every mode (Grey/94 in light, Grey/20 in dark). The distinction is semantic: Surface/RaisedBase names the screen-level surface — the background a screen presents when its content sits alongside other non-grouped elements on the same fill. Surface/RaisedSecondary names the component-level surface — chips, badges, and small contained UI. Picking the right token lets either side change independently in the future.

5 canonical stroke roles

The stroke layer is a 5-token ladder, each with a distinct job and a real perceptual gap. Pick the lightest stroke that still reads against the surface beneath it.

TokenLightDarkJobHandles
Stroke/Divider Grey/88 Grey/24 Quiet, always-on separation Row dividers, section breaks, horizontal rules inside a container
Stroke/Elevated (outside) Grey/82 Grey/30 Mid-weight, holds against varied backdrops Floating + Overlay surface edges
Stroke/Container (outer) Grey/76 Grey/30 Balanced container border, readable on any common surface Card edges on Canvas, Base, Sunken, RaisedSecondary, RaisedPrimary
Stroke/ContainerRaised Grey/74 Grey/38 Stronger container border for darker raised surfaces Borders on chips, badges, reaction pills, small components against any dark raised surface
Stroke/Accessible Grey/38 Grey/68 High-contrast outline Inputs, focus rings, anything requiring guaranteed visibility
Container vs Divider: Container reads distinctly darker than Divider in light mode (Grey/76 vs Grey/88) and slightly lighter in dark (Grey/30 vs Grey/24) — restores a visible Container > Divider hierarchy in both themes. Semantically: Divider is the separator inside a container (rows, sections), Container is the border around the container.

4 container roles

Paired tokens for grouped-list patterns. The Primary pair is the subtle/recessed treatment — in light mode the Container reads slightly darker than its Base (card sinks into the page), in dark mode the Container reads slightly lighter (card lifts off the page). The Secondary pair is the iOS systemGroupedBackground / secondarySystemGroupedBackground contrast pattern — a tinted page with a clearly lifted white card on top.

RoleLight L1Dark L1Purpose
Surface/Group/Primary/Base Grey/100 Grey/10 Page behind the subtle/recessed container pattern. White in light mode, soft dark grey in dark mode.
Surface/Group/Primary/Container Grey/94 Grey/20 Card on top of Primary/Base. In light mode reads as slightly recessed (Grey/94 on Grey/100); in dark mode reads as slightly lifted (Grey/20 on Grey/10). Subtle hierarchy.
Surface/Group/Secondary/Base Grey/94 Grey/10 Tinted page for the iOS-style grouped list. Light tint of Grey/94 in light mode, soft dark Grey/10 in dark mode.
Surface/Group/Secondary/Container Grey/100 Grey/18 Lifted card on top of Secondary/Base. White in light mode (the iOS secondarySystemGroupedBackground equivalent), Grey/18 in dark mode (one step lifted off Base Grey/10).
When to reach for which pair: use the Primary pair for sheets, floating panels, and contexts where the card should read as a subtle inset or quiet step on the page (Container is darker than Base in light, lifted in dark). Use the Secondary pair for Settings-style screens, profile detail views, and other iOS-faithful grouped layouts where the tinted page reads as recessed beneath a clearly elevated white card.

2 platform-chrome roles

Exceptions to the canonical system — for OS-targeted styling.

RolePurpose
Surface/DominantTop chrome / header layer where titles and filters live. iOS 26 navigation may impose its own material.
Surface/QuaternaryBottom tab bar surface. iOS and Android may impose blur or tint materials.

4 specialty roles

Purpose-built surfaces for specific UI states — voice/calling indicators, translucent button materials, translucent container fills, and the tertiary raised tier.

RoleValuePurpose
Surface/ActiveSpeaker #9EA2FF Voice/calling — the highlight ring or fill on the active speaker tile during a call. Single hex across both themes; the meaning is identical regardless of mode.
Surface/BtntAlpha #292929 α78% Translucent button surface — the iOS-style hold-to-reveal button overlay used for floating action affordances. Identical across modes by design.
Surface/ContainerAlpha White α88% / #292929 α88% Use for translucent surfaces — White α88% in light, #292929 α88% in dark. Ideal for cards floating over content that must remain partly visible; pair with backdrop-filter: blur for the iOS-native frosted effect.
Surface/RaisedTertiary Grey/96 (#F5F5F5) / Grey/10 (#1A1A1A) The lightest raised surface, for large containers such as grouped lists or tile buttons. Synced with Surface/Group/Primary/Container — both roles represent the same tonal step at different structural positions.
Note on Surface/Group/*/Base tokens. Surface/Group/Primary/Base and Surface/Group/Secondary/Base currently resolve to fully transparent (#ffffff @ α0). They exist as structural placeholders inside the Group container pattern — the visible surface is the /Container child, and the /Base role is a hook for future tinted-page treatments. Treat them as no-op backgrounds today.

Axis 2 — Environment Levels

Environment levels describe whether a surface is in the root app environment or an elevated container.

L1

Root Application Environment

The base canvas of the app. Used for main screens, root tabs, and the primary app canvas.

L2

Elevated Canvas Environment

Used when the canvas itself becomes elevated. Specifically: bottom sheets, modal flows, drawer content, and expanded elevated experiences.

Important distinction. L2 is only for canvas-elevated environments. Floating temporary UI is not L2 — menus, popovers, reaction pickers, and tooltips all use Surface/Floating regardless of whether the parent environment is L1 or L2.
Overlay content must be set to L2. When a frame sits inside a Surface/Overlay — modal sheets, drawer content, the body of an alert — its mode must be set to Dark L2 (or Light L2). Overlay in dark mode resolves to the same value as Canvas L2 (#1a1a1a); leaving the modal content on Dark L1 causes nested surfaces to lose contrast against the Overlay, and Surface/Group/Primary/Base becomes mathematically invisible (1.00:1 ratio). See the Elevation page for the full diagram and the math.
Concept

How the Two Axes Combine #

The semantic role determines which token a designer picks. The environment level determines which tonal value that token resolves to at runtime — controlled by the mode set on the parent frame.

A Surface/Floating placed inside an L1 frame and a Surface/Floating placed inside an L2 frame both express the same intent ("floating temporary UI surface"). The tonal value may shift between L1 and L2 to keep the surface perceptually lifted against its host canvas — in dark mode Floating steps from Grey/22 to Grey/24, while in light mode it stays Grey/100 in both environments (pure white already reads as fully elevated against either light canvas).

The semantic name never changes. Only the contextual modifier (L1 vs L2) shifts.
Surface/Floating + Parent frame mode ↓ Resolved tonal value
Reference

The Four Modes #

The Monocore Semantic collection has four modes that combine theme and environment. A designer sets the mode on the parent frame. Every variable-bound surface inside automatically resolves to the right value.

Light L1
Light theme, root environment
Light L2
Light theme, elevated environment
Dark L1
Dark theme, root environment
Dark L2
Dark theme, elevated environment
Implementation

Layered Architecture #

The system is built in three layers: Layer 1 holds raw primitive values; Layer 2 holds purpose-named semantic tokens (Theme (Light - dark)) with two modes — Light and Dark; Layer 3 is a Figma extension of Theme (Modal (Light - dark)) that inherits every variable and overrides only the ~30 tokens that need to shift when content sits inside a modal, sheet, or overlay context.

Layer 1 — Primitives

Global collection · single mode

Raw color values with no theme awareness. 90 color primitives + 21 spacing primitives (111 total) spanning the neutral ramp, alpha tokens, brand ramps, status palettes, and special-purpose colors:

  • Fluent 2/Grey/0 through Fluent 2/Grey/100 — 26 stops on the Fluent 2 neutral ramp
  • Fluent 2/Alpha/* — 9 tokens (Black α7/12/40/60, White α4/13/24, plus Transparent & Clear)
  • Global colors/Brand/Teams 10 through Teams 160 — 16 stops on the Fluent 2 brandTeams ramp, exposed as first-class primitives. Three stops carry semantic labels: Teams 60 (text-icons), Teams 80 (Primary), Teams 100 (dPrimary - text). Semantic tokens like Text/Interactive can alias directly to these instead of going through Brand light/Primary AA.
  • Brand light/* · Brand dark/* — 10 + 9 stops that mirror the Teams ramp at the same luminance points, plus the Primary AA variant for AA-compliant text. Retained for backwards compatibility; new consumers should alias the Teams ramp directly.
  • Danger light/* · Danger dark/* — 5 + 5 stops including the Primary AA variants
  • Success light/dark · Warning light/dark · Saved light/dark — 2 each
  • Mention/Primary · DropCall/Primary — single-tone primitives shared across themes
111 primitives (90 color + 21 spacing)
Layer 2 — Semantic (Theme)

Theme (Light - dark) collection · 2 modes · 247 variables total

Purpose-named tokens that alias primitives differently per Light / Dark mode. This is the base layer designers and components bind to. Every semantic token holds a VARIABLE_ALIAS reference to a primitive. The core Surface + Text + Icon + Stroke families total 72 roles; the remaining 175 variables cover Brand/Accent tiers, Component tokens, Presence, iOS Fills, and os26 material effects:

  • Surface — 34 roles (Canvas / Group Primary/Secondary / RaisedBase / RaisedPrimary / RaisedSecondary / RaisedTertiary / Floating / Overlay / Sunken / Interactive / status surfaces / Accent / DropCall / ActiveSpeaker / BtntAlpha / ContainerAlpha / Glass / Scrim)
  • Text — 18 roles (Dominant / Primary / Secondary / Hint / Disabled / On Global / On Accent / Interactive / Link / Assistive / Carret / Mention / Danger / Success / Warning / Alt Secondary / Highlighted Background / Highlighted Foreground)
  • Icon — 14 roles (Dominant / Primary / Secondary / Hint / Disabled / On Global / On Accent / Interactive / Danger / Success / Warning / Alt Secondary / Mention / Saved)
  • Stroke — 6 roles (Divider / Accessible / Elevated (outside) / Container (outer) / ContainerRaised / onMedia (outer))
  • Other — 175 additional semantic tokens across Brand/Accent tiers, Component tokens, Presence, iOS Fills, and os26 material effects
247 semantic variables · 72 core roles + 175 extended
Layer 3 — Modal Extension

Modal (Light - dark) collection · Figma extension of Theme

An extended collection created via Figma's Extend action. Modal inherits every variable from Theme automatically — 217 tokens fall through unchanged. Only 30 tokens carry explicit overrides for the elevated context (Overlay, Sheets, Drawers, Modals). Bind a modal frame to Modal to get all Theme values plus the elevated overrides.

30 overrides · 217 inherited from Theme
Primitives (111) ↓ VARIABLE_ALIAS Theme (247 × Light + Dark) ↓ Extend Modal (30 overrides + inherits Theme) ↓ Mode on parent frame Rendered surface
Rationale

Why This Works #

For the design system

Semantic names plus mode-aware aliases mean a component built today on Surface/RaisedBase keeps rendering correctly even when the underlying greys are refined, themes are added (high-contrast, glass), or new environment levels are introduced as future modes.

Components encode purpose, not pixels.

For code generation

The structure maps cleanly onto a deterministic plan: primitives are leaves, semantics are recipes that pick a leaf based on a single context input (mode). One enum, one lookup, no conditional logic.

Components encode what they want, the system encodes how to deliver it.

Semantic Surface System

Corner radius

A discrete radius scale that maps every UI surface to a consistent corner. Container-level surfaces round to the medium step; embedded elements pick up a smaller step; pill-shaped controls take the full-round token.

Discrete scale Surface → radius
Foundations

Radius scale #

Seven named radius tokens describe the curve's character on an intensity ladder. prominent (16) is the most-used radius — it covers most components. When components appear together, a shared radius makes them read as a family rather than a collection. Choose a wider radius only for the largest containers, and a smaller one only when a nested element needs to read as a step inside its parent.

TokenValueUse it forWhy
rounded9999Pills and full circles — avatars, badges, action chips, reaction pills.Maximum curve. Resolves to a half-pill at runtime once one axis caps the other.
dominant24The largest cards — Post feed cards, hero cards, feature surfaces.The wider curve lets a dominant surface read distinctly from the components nested inside it.
prominent · Baseline16Most components — cards, panels, sheets, chiclets, grouped containers, the bulk of the system.A shared radius binds adjacent components into a coherent group.
strong12Nested items inside a prominent-radius parent.One step inside 16. Reads as contained without competing with the parent.
default8Smaller nested components, or compact controls where strong still feels too soft.Tightens the curve when content is dense.
minimal4The smallest details.The minimum that still reads as intentionally rounded rather than square.
None0Squared corners — structural dividers, full-bleed separators, content that should not read as rounded at all.No softening; explicit absence of curve.
Naming note: the token named default resolves to 8, not the most-used radius. prominent (16) is the most-used. The names describe the curve's character on the intensity ladder — not which value is the most-applied default. Reach for the role that matches your component's intent, not the token whose name says "default."
Group by meaning, scope by update target. Names organize tokens by the role they serve, and by the bundle that needs to change together. A radius token isn't called 16 — it carries the name of the role it represents, so refining the standard component radius across the system happens in one place.

Spacing tokens (Size, Nudge, and the Combined nudge + regular ramp) live on their own page. See Spacing.

Semantic Surface System

Spacing

A direction-agnostic ramp for gaps between elements, a separate ramp for optical nudges against forced-padding containers, and a combined ramp that pre-computes the useful sums of the two — so Figma bindings stay one variable per property even when the intent is "regular step plus a nudge."

8 Size tokens 4 Nudge tokens 10 Combined tokens
Foundations

Spacing ramp #

The full direction-agnostic ramp. Eight t-shirt sizes from none to xxxlarge, each step sitting on a multiple of 4 from 4 to 32 with 0 as the anchor. Use the same token whether you're spacing items vertically in a list or horizontally in a row.

TokenValueUse it for
Size/none0Stacked elements that read as a single unit — avatar & name, title & subtitle with no breathing room.
Size/xsmall4The tightest meaningful gap. Inline labels and their adjacent icons.
Size/small8Groups that call for a tighter rhythm than the default. Compact rows, dense controls.
Size/medium12Default for grouped components stacked vertically. Accommodates the prominent (16) corner radius — adjacent corners don't collide.
Size/large16One step looser than the default. Section breaks within a larger group.
Size/xlarge20Stronger separation between content blocks.
Size/xxlarge24Hierarchy-level separation — between distinct content regions on a screen.
Size/xxxlarge32The widest standard gap. Top-of-screen padding, page-level section dividers.
Practice

Vertical spacing — in practice #

Grouped components sit 12 apart by default. The default corner radius needs room to breathe — 12 keeps adjacent surfaces from visually colliding at their curves. Step down to 8 when a tighter rhythm reads better. For vertically stacked text, use 0 or 2.

SpacingUse it forWhy
12 · defaultGrouped components stacked vertically.Accommodates the 16 radius — adjacent corners don't collide.
8Groups that call for a tighter rhythm.The next step down when 12 leaves too much air.
2Vertically stacked text where the lines still need to separate visually.A hairline gap — reads as paired but distinct.
0Vertically stacked text that reads as a single unit — for example, an avatar & name group.No gap; the lines belong together.
Foundations

Nudge #

A separate four-step ramp for fine alignment — the tiny offsets needed to optically center icons or align content with ghost buttons that have forced container padding. These sit on the off-beat between the main spacing values (2, 6, 10), giving designers a controlled set of micro-adjustments without inventing one-off numbers.

TokenValueUse it for
Size/Nudge/none0The baseline — no adjustment.
Size/Nudge/small2The smallest visual nudge. Hairline alignment between icons and adjacent labels.
Size/Nudge/medium6Mid-range optical alignment — counteracting the forced padding inside an icon or ghost-button container.
Size/Nudge/large10The largest nudge. Used where a component's internal padding pushes content noticeably off-grid.
Reference

Combined — nudge + regular #

Figma's variable binding doesn't allow two variables added together in a single property, so when a designer needs a padding value that's conceptually a regular ramp step plus a nudge (e.g. an icon's internal 2dp nudge plus an 8dp gap to the next element), there's no way to express that as the sum of two bindings — it has to be one token. The combined ramp pre-computes the ten useful sums of nudge × regular and names each one with the formula so engineers and designers can both read the intent off the token.

TokenSumReads as
Size/Combined/2ng + 4rg6dpHairline nudge + xsmall gap.
Size/Combined/2ng + 8rg10dpHairline nudge + small gap.
Size/Combined/2ng + 12rg14dpHairline nudge + default medium gap.
Size/Combined/2ng + 16rg18dpHairline nudge + large gap.
Size/Combined/2ng + 20rg22dpHairline nudge + xlarge gap.
Size/Combined/2ng + 24rg26dpHairline nudge + xxlarge gap.
Size/Combined/6ng + 24rg30dpMid-range nudge + xxlarge gap.
Size/Combined/2ng + 32rg34dpHairline nudge + xxxlarge gap.
Size/Combined/6ng + 32rg38dpMid-range nudge + xxxlarge gap.
Size/Combined/10ng + 32rg42dpLargest nudge + xxxlarge gap.
Naming convention. {N}ng is the nudge value in dp (2ng, 6ng, 10ng from the Nudge ramp). {M}rg is the regular ramp value in dp (4rg through 32rg from the Spacing ramp). The token's resolved value is the sum, aliased to the corresponding Size/{sum}dp primitive.
Deduplication rule — bigger rg wins. Several sums can be reached by more than one formula (e.g. 10dp could be 2ng + 8rg or 6ng + 4rg). The published token at each sum uses the formula with the largest regular value, since that reads more naturally as "a real spacing step with a small nudge correction" than as "a tiny base step with heavy nudging." So 10dp ships as 2ng + 8rg, 14dp as 2ng + 12rg, and so on — one token per sum, no formula ambiguity.

Spacing · Semantic Surface System · 8 Size · 4 Nudge · 10 Combined
Spacing

Architecture

Concept

Why three ramps #

Most spacing decisions are about gaps — how far one element sits from the next. That's the Size ramp. But two other situations come up often enough to deserve their own scales: micro-adjustments to optically align content against a container that has forced padding (Nudge), and the case where Figma's one-variable-per-property limit forces a designer to pre-compute the sum of a Size and a Nudge as a single named token (Combined).

Spacing vs Nudge. Use Size/* for gaps between elements — this is most spacing. Use Size/Nudge/* for optical adjustments inside or against a component that has forced padding (an icon, a ghost button) where the standard ramp would over- or under-correct. If you're nudging anything that isn't an icon or ghost-padded container, you probably want a Spacing token instead.

Migration Guide · Usage-based mapping

Teams 2 → Monocore Colour Mapping

Every colour token in Teams 2 Mobile Variables (111 in the Color collection) is mapped below to a Monocore Canvas L1 semantic by where it is actually bound in the Teams 2 iOS components, then checked against where the Monocore iOS Toolkit binds its own semantics and against the Monocore migration rules. 79 of the old tokens resolve to a single Monocore semantic (40 confirmed by observed use, 39 never bound in a component and matched by value and description); 13 split by context and need a conditional rule; 18 have no Monocore target (7 of them are broken alpha tokens that resolve to white); 1 is a mode pin rather than a token.

111 old tokens2,330 old bindings read4,870 Monocore bindings readOctober 2026
Reference

How to read this #

Each row is derived from bindings, not names: the Observed use column is where the old token is bound inside the Teams 2 iOS component library (component set, layer, and whether the binding is a fill, stroke or text), and the Monocore target is the semantic that the Monocore iOS Toolkit binds in the equivalent component and layer. Counts are component-library bindings (instances excluded), so they measure design intent rather than screen volume.

MatchMeaning
1:1One Monocore semantic serves every observed use. Values may shift (Teams 2 greys were v900/v500; Monocore greys are 24/61) — those shifts are listed, not hidden.
SplitThe old token did two or more jobs that Monocore separates. The row names each job and its target; the rule lives in the Conditional rules table.
Mode, not tokenThe old token encoded a fixed appearance (always-dark calling chrome). Monocore expresses this by pinning the frame's mode, not by a token.
StaysSame name exists in Monocore and carries the same role; migration is a re-import of the key (the Monocore migration page marks these as awaiting a future State/* layer).
NoneNo Monocore semantic serves the role yet. The row says what to do meanwhile.
UnusedNot bound anywhere in the Teams 2 iOS component library, so there is no usage evidence; the target is by value and description only.

Where this mapping disagrees with the published Teams Migration rules on the Monocore docs site, the row says so and gives the usage evidence; the two disagreements are Surface/Subtle Fill and Surface/Quaternary.

Reference

Surfaces #

Four of the old surface tokens were doing several jobs each; Monocore gives each job its own semantic. The old library had no concept of a floating surface, a scrim, or L1/L2 elevation, so those targets are new roles rather than renames.

Surface/Subtle means “inherit the parent’s colour” in code. It is alpha 0 in every mode, so a layer bound to it has no colour of its own in Figma. When a mapping below lands on Surface/Subtle (list rows, section headers, carousel buttons, command-bar buttons, transparent grouping), the iOS and Android implementation should set no background and let the parent surface show through, not paint a transparent colour. It is the one target in this document that is an instruction to engineering rather than a colour.

Strokes, dividers and borders #

Teams 2 had one divider colour and used it for everything from list separators to text-field underlines. Monocore publishes a stroke ladder (Divider → Container → ContainerRaised → Accessible) plus alpha strokes for media and floating surfaces, so the mapping depends on what the line is separating.

The docs assign input outlines to Stroke/Accessible; note the Monocore Text Field still carries the old Divider/Primary on its underline (see Gaps).

1 binding: Button Full-width outlineStroke/ContainerRaised (neutral outline) or Brand/Accent Secondary (accent outline)SplitMonocore’s Button Style=Outline accent binds Surface/RaisedSecondary fill with Text/Primary label and ContainerRaised stroke (13); Split Button keeps the accent-tinted Brand/Accent Secondary stroke (33). Pick by whether the button family is neutral or accent.
Component tokens/Button/Button Stroke outline pressed, Button fg outline pressedNot bound in componentsBrand/Accent Secondary (stroke) / Text/Interactive (label)UnusedMonocore has no pressed-outline token; pressed state is expressed by Surface/SubtleSelected fill behind the same stroke.

Stroke notes (from the Monocore Variables descriptions).

  • Stroke/ContainerRaised — stronger container border for elements that need maximum visibility against darker raised surfaces: chips, badges, reaction pills, small floating elements, and any component edge that must clear AA contrast on top of RaisedPrimary or RaisedSecondary where Stroke/Container would be too subtle. Light Grey/74 (L1) / Grey/68 (L2); Dark Grey/38 (L1) / Grey/42 (L2). For standard container borders on lighter surfaces use Stroke/Container; for inputs and focus rings use Stroke/Accessible.
  • Stroke/Floating — separation stroke for elevated and transient surfaces (Floating and Overlay): popovers, menus, sheets. Mid-weight so it holds against the varied content behind them.
  • Stroke/onMedia — alpha-based outer stroke for images and other variable-content surfaces (aliases Fluent 2/Alpha primitives; resolved luminance matches the divider stroke per mode on the standard backdrop). Over an image the alpha lets the pixels show through so the edge blends instead of reading as a hard grey line. Implement with outer stroke placement, never inner.

Text and Icon #

Text and Icon tokens migrate by name: Monocore kept the whole set and binds them on the same layer roles (Text/Secondary on captions, timestamps and sublabels; Text/Primary on titles and labels; Text/On Accent on badge and accent-button labels). Rules

Conditional rules #

These are the rules a rebind script (or a designer) applies when the old token alone does not decide the target. Each rule is evaluated top-down on the bound layer: first by the component it sits in, then by the layer’s role, then by node type; the last row of each group is the default.

Audit

Gaps #

Old tokens with no Monocore semantic. Brand-tinted “me” chat bubble (Notification bg dominant alt1); the three AI liveness colours; Avatar/Inside stroke, Background and Foreground from the Avatar colour library (both libraries still bind these directly — leave them); the five iOS Systems/Notifications colour styles on the Incoming Call component; Light theme/TMS Tint10 on the Fab title; Colors/Neutral/Grey/18 on the card live indicator. These match the 14 deferred variables in the migration audit and should stay on a manual-fix list rather than be rebound by rule.

Roles Monocore adds that Teams 2 never had. Surface/SubtleHover, Surface/Floating + Stroke/Floating, Surface/Scrim, Surface/Sunken, Surface/Interactive, Surface/Glass, the InsetGroup Base/Container pairs, Surface/RaisedTertiary and RaisedDominant, Stroke/Accessible, Stroke/onMedia, Text/Mention, Icon/Dominant Invert. A migrated screen will not pick these up automatically; they appear only when the component is rebuilt on Monocore.

Old bindings still live inside the Monocore iOS Toolkit. The usage scan found these component layers still bound to the old Color collection rather than Canvas L1; they are the places where a Monocore component will render an old value:

Method

Sources #

  • Old tokens: Teams 2 Mobile Variables — Color collection, 111 variables, Light/Dark values resolved through their Global aliases.
  • Old usage: Teams 2 iOS — 42 component pages, every fill and stroke binding on component-owned layers (nested instance internals excluded), 2,330 bindings across 73 distinct variables.
  • New usage: Monocore iOS Toolkit — 48 component pages, same method, 4,870 bindings across 113 Canvas L1 semantics.
  • New semantics and values: Monocore Variables (FuEZCHmjZMYpCpPpdkNmJj), Canvas L1 collection.
  • Rules: Teams Migration — Token Mappings and Semantic Surface System on the Monocore docs site.

Method: for each old variable, the component set, layer name and paint role of every binding were tallied; the Monocore target is the semantic bound on the equivalent component and layer in the Toolkit. A target was accepted as 1:1 only when one Monocore semantic covered every observed use; otherwise the uses were split and each given its own rule. Name similarity was used only to label the Stays rows, never to choose a target.

Semantic Surface System

Text & Icon

The Text/* and Icon/* roles carry forward from the prior color system. They were not remapped by the Monocore migration — the names stay, the values were ported to Fluent 2 / Grey primitives where appropriate, and the branded / status / mention-style roles still alias the same Brand and Danger sources they always did.

18 text roles 14 icon roles Carried forward

Text & Icon

Guidance

Behavior

Behavioral notes #

Text and Icon are paired by purpose, not by value. Text/Primary and Icon/Primary describe the same role (standard foreground at standard emphasis) but pick slightly different greys per mode. Use the Text token on text and the Icon token on icons — do not cross-bind them.
Secondary stepping is now aligned across Text and Icon. Icon/Secondary and Icon/Hint previously inverted the L1/L2 step pattern relative to Text/Secondary on the principle that icons survive at lower contrast than running text. After the accessibility audit, that assumption failed in practice — icons at Grey/56 against raised dark surfaces dropped below 3:1. Both now alias the same Grey primitives as Text/Secondary (Grey/38 L1, Grey/24 L2 light; Grey/68 across dark). Text and Icon Secondary now resolve to identical hexes per mode.
The hardcoded status hex values are temporary. Text/Success, Text/Warning, Icon/Success, and Icon/Warning carry baked-in hex pairs pending the State/* token layer. Icon/Mention and Icon/Saved follow the same pattern. When State lands these will become aliases.

Architecture

Scope

What's on this page #

The Surface migration repointed every neutral grey to the Fluent 2 ramp and reorganized the canonical surface roles. The Text and Icon layers were treated as carried-forward — the role names and consumer bindings did not change, only the underlying primitives. This page documents the resulting tables so the active values are explicit.

Naming carries forward; values were ported. Where a Text or Icon role aliased a neutral grey (e.g. Text/Primary, Icon/Disabled), the alias now points at the corresponding Fluent 2/Grey/N primitive. Where the role aliased a brand or danger color, the binding is unchanged.

Theming

Theming lets a product swap its brand color set without touching any component. The five Brand/Accent * tokens are the semantic layer products bind to; the values resolve from the active brand palette in Global colors/Brand light and Brand dark, which themselves are owned by the Brand collection and can be repointed per product.

5 accent roles 9 modes Brand-swappable
Reference

The Accent ladder #

Five tiers from most prominent to barely-there. Each row shows the brand-palette tint/shade that the token aliases in each theme. Light-mode rows show Brand light/*; dark-mode rows show Brand dark/*.

TokenLight L1 / L2Dark L1 / L2Role
Brand/Accent Dominant Brand light/Shade 10 Brand dark/Shade 30 Most emphasized branded surface. The darkest shade in light mode, the lightest in dark.
Brand/Accent Primary Brand light/Primary Brand dark/Primary Canonical brand color. Logo fills, primary buttons, key brand surfaces.
Brand/Accent Secondary Brand light/Tint 30 Brand dark/Tint 30 Supporting branded surface. One step subtler than Primary.
Brand/Accent Tertiary Brand light/Tint 50 Brand dark/Tint 40 Ambient branded wash. Page tints, subtle brand presence.
Brand/Accent Quaternary Brand light/Tint 50 Brand dark/Tint 40 Barely-there branded wash. Currently shares values with Tertiary — a distinct primitive can be introduced later without renaming consumers.
Quaternary and Tertiary currently resolve to the same primitive. The brand palette tops out at Tint 50 (light) and Tint 40 (dark). Quaternary exists to give designers a slot for the very lightest branded wash; until a distinct primitive is added it inherits Tertiary's values. The semantic name lets consumers bind today and pick up the divergent value automatically when it lands.
Related

Related Brand tokens #

The Accent ladder is the canonical theming surface, but two related tokens carry over from the prior system:

TokenLight / DarkPurpose
Brand/Accent GlobalBrand light/Shade 10 · Brand dark/Tint 20Cross-theme brand stamp — used in places that need a consistent brand color regardless of L1/L2. Pre-dates the Dominant tier; consider migrating consumers to Brand/Accent Dominant.
Surface/AccentBrand light/Primary · Brand dark/PrimaryBranded surface fill — the surface itself, not text/icons over it. Pair with Text/On Accent and Icon/On Accent for legible content.
Voice & Calling

Voice & Calling surfaces #

Two semantic surfaces carry the affordance language for voice and calling UI — the primary action (answer, mute toggle, raise hand) and the destructive action (end call, decline, hang up). Both surfaces have purpose-named bindings so the call experience can be re-themed without touching neutral surfaces.

TokenLightDarkUsed for
Surface/Accent Brand light/Primary · #654CF5 Brand dark/Primary · #8A80FF Primary affirmative call actions — Answer, Accept, Raise Hand, Mute toggle (active), Camera (active), Share. Pair with Text/On Accent and Icon/On Accent for legible labels.
Surface/DropCall DropCall/Primary · #932F2F DropCall/Primary · #932F2F Destructive call actions — End Call, Decline, Hang Up, Leave Meeting. Pair with white text/icons (Text/On Global, Icon/On Global) for a consistent destructive affordance.
DropCall is single-tone across themes. Unlike the rest of the colored surface system, Surface/DropCall resolves to the same hex (#932F2F) in every light and dark mode. The destructive-call affordance is a learned interaction — users associate the specific red with "End Call." Shifting it between themes would dilute that recognition. The dark-mode value sits at the same saturation as the light-mode value because the contrast against white text (Text/On Global) is what matters, not the visual relationship to the canvas behind it.
Both surfaces are FRAME_FILL-scoped. Bind them on the parent button/container frame fill, not on text or strokes. Foreground content sits on top using the On Accent / On Global roles.

Primitive layering

Both Voice & Calling surfaces alias dedicated Global primitives, matching the pattern used for the Brand and Status families:

  • Surface/Accent → Global colors/Brand light/Primary · Global colors/Brand dark/Primary — shared with the brand identity.
  • Surface/DropCall → Global colors/DropCall/Primary — voice-and-calling-specific, single value across themes.
Brand primitives

Teams brand ramp #

The Teams brand palette lives in the Global collection as sixteen first-class primitives at Global colors/Brand/Teams 10 through Teams 160. These are the source of truth for the brand identity — the older Brand light/* and Brand dark/* primitives mirror the Teams ramp at the same luminance points but are retained mostly for backwards compatibility. New semantic tokens should alias the Teams primitives directly.

PrimitiveHexSemantic roleUsed by

Teams 20#2F2A5E—Brand light/Shade 20 & 30, Brand dark/Tint 40 & 50 mirror this stop.
Teams 30#332D6E—Brand dark/Tint 30.
Teams 40#3A3082—Brand light/Shade 10 mirrors this stop.
Teams 50#43349C—Brand dark/Tint 20.
Teams 60 (text-icons)#4C39B8Interactive text-icon colorText/Interactive, Text/Link, Text/Assistive alias this stop in Light. The "(text-icons)" label denotes its intended semantic role.
Teams 70#5A40DBPrimary AABrand light/Primary AA mirrors this stop. Icon/Interactive, Text/Carret, Text/Mention alias here.
Teams 80 (Primary)#654CF5Brand Primary (light theme)Surface/Accent aliases this stop in Light. The canonical light-theme brand color.
Teams 90#7769FA—Brand light/Tint 10 mirrors this stop.
Teams 100 (dPrimary - text)#8A80FFBrand Primary (dark theme, text)Surface/Accent and Text/Interactive, Text/Link, Text/Assistive alias this stop in Dark. Named "(dPrimary - text)" for its dark-theme text role.
Teams 110#9994FF—Brand light/Tint 20, Brand dark/Shade 10 mirror this stop.
Teams 120#ABA8FFShade 20 (dark theme)Brand dark/Shade 20 mirrors this stop. Icon/Interactive, Text/Carret, Text/Mention alias here in Dark.
Teams 130#BAB8FF—Unused today — available for future brand tier.

Two aliasing paths, same source. Semantic tokens that reference brand color arrive at the same hex via two routes: the direct path aliases Global colors/Brand/Teams N (e.g. Text/Interactive → Teams 60); the legacy path aliases Brand light/* or Brand dark/* (e.g. Text/Carret → Brand light/Primary AA). Because the two ramps mirror each other at matching luminance points, both routes resolve to the same or very close hex. New tokens should prefer the direct Teams path.
Three stops carry semantic labels in their name. Teams 60 is text-icons, Teams 80 is Primary, Teams 100 is dPrimary - text. Those labels are shorthand for the role the stop was designed to fill: an interactive text-icon color at the darkest legible point (60), the canonical brand color at mid-ramp (80), and the dark-theme text-safe brand at high-brightness (100).

Theming

Guidance

Workflow

Swapping the active palette #

A product can ship multiple brand palettes (e.g. Teams default, partner co-brand, seasonal palette) and swap the active one at runtime. The Accent tokens never change; the palette they alias to does.

  1. Define palettes in the Brand collection. Each palette is a complete set of Brand light/* and Brand dark/* primitives.
  2. Bind components to Brand/Accent *. Components never reference the palette directly.
  3. At runtime, point the Accent tokens at the chosen palette. Every consumer updates without recompiling.
  4. Add new palettes by extending the Brand collection. The Accent ladder doesn't change shape.

Theming

Architecture

Concept

How theming works #

The Accent ladder describes the role of a branded surface or fill — "most prominent," "standard," "subtle," and so on — without committing to a specific color. The active brand palette (set by the product) supplies the underlying hex values. Switch the palette and every Accent consumer follows; rename the role and you've made a single coordinated update across every consuming component.

Semantic ladder, palette-driven values. Components bind to Brand/Accent Primary, not to Brand light/Primary. The active palette decides what "Primary" resolves to. A Teams build can swap the palette without recompiling components.
Behavior

Across modes #

Accent tokens are mode-aware in the same sense as the Surface ladder. L1 and L2 resolve to the same value (the brand palette is environment-independent); the L1 IC and L2 IC modes mirror their non-IC counterparts; the Glass (WIP) mode currently inherits the light-mode value. Light/dark inversion is handled by the brand palette itself: Brand light/* and Brand dark/* are distinct primitives, each tuned for legibility in its own theme.

Don't bind directly to brand primitives. Components reach for Brand/Accent Primary, not Brand light/Primary. Direct binding to the palette bypasses the semantic layer and breaks the swap-the-palette story.

Semantic Surface System

Scaling Rules

A two-part framework for Dynamic Type. First, classify each component into a scale tier that sets how much its text is allowed to grow (Scale0, Scale1, ScaleMax). Then, at the upper bound of that tier, use reflow tokens to decide what happens to elements that still won't fit — extending vertically (extend0–extendFit) or stacking columns (virticalStack).

3 scale tiers 5 reflow tokens iOS & Android
Foundations

Scale tiers #

Each component belongs to one of three tiers based on how much its text is allowed to grow. The tier sets the ceiling; the reflow tokens decide what happens at that ceiling.

TierMaximum scaleUse it for
Scale01× · no scaleComponents whose text content is always the same and lives in the same location. Tab bars, fixed labels in chrome that the user reads at a glance, content anchored to a UI region rather than to body text.
Scale11.3× · capped scalingComponents whose text lives in the same location and doesn't change often. Headers, search placeholders, badges, token fields, message-compose chrome — text that's allowed to grow somewhat while the surrounding container stays usable.
ScaleMaxUnrestrictedComponents whose text is the user's content — chat list items, message bodies, anything the user reads attentively. Scale continues to the full Dynamic Type ceiling; reflow tokens take over from there.
Pick the tier from the role, not the size. The question is "what does this text do?" — chrome (Scale0), navigation or container labels (Scale1), user content (ScaleMax) — not "how big do I want it to be."
Reflow

Reflow tokens — extending lines #

At the upper bound of Scale1 and ScaleMax — the max zoom level where comprehension is already constrained — four extend tokens control how many additional lines a text element is allowed to wrap to before truncating. Assign the token per text element; the cell as a whole inherits the most permissive value of its children.

TokenValueBehavior
extend0Plus 0No lines added. The text truncates at its original line count.
extend1Plus 1Add one more line before truncating.
extend2Plus 2Add two more lines before truncating.
extendFitUnboundNever truncate. Let all text reflow into as many lines as it needs.
Pick the smallest extend that preserves the message. A timestamp doesn't need extendFit; a primary message label might. Defaulting every element to extendFit defeats the framework — every cell takes unbounded vertical space and pushes the next cell off-screen.
Reflow

Reflow tokens — stacking columns #

When the extend tokens still aren't enough — typically because the leading column has grown so wide it begins to clip the trailing column — the trailing column reflows beneath the leading column instead of competing with it for horizontal space.

TokenBehavior
virticalStack (sic — token name as published)When the leading column begins to clip the trailing column, reflow the trailing column under the leading column.

This gives each cell two degrees of freedom at max zoom: vertical expansion within the original row (the extend tokens), and column-stacking once horizontal space is exhausted (virticalStack). Together they let a chat row with a long message and a long timestamp degrade gracefully instead of overlapping.

The order of fallback. The extend tokens are tried first — they preserve the two-column layout. virticalStack is the second step, only reached when the trailing column still can't fit. Two cascading fallbacks, applied in sequence by the framework.
Platform implementation

iOS implementation #

iOS doesn't use a decimal scaling factor. Each component opts into one of four UIContentSizeCategory strategies that govern the band of allowed text sizes under the user's Dynamic Type setting. The framework tiers (Scale0, Scale1, ScaleMax) map onto these strategies as follows.

The four iOS strategies

Each strategy defines a min and max content size category. Sizes outside the band are clamped to the bound. The five accessibility categories (AX1–AX5) are only reachable when the user enables Larger Accessibility Sizes in iOS Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size.

iOS strategy Range What it does
default xSmall → AX5 Follows the user's device setting with no upper bound. Text scales through every category including all five accessibility sizes.
large xSmall → Large Min is unbounded; max preferred size is Large (the system default). Components grow from the smallest scale up to Large and stop.
excludeAccessibilityCategory xSmall → xxxLarge Caps at xxxLarge — the largest non-accessibility size. AX1–AX5 never reshape the layout.
largeToExcludeAccessibilityCategory Large → xxxLarge Floored at Large, capped at xxxLarge. Text never goes below the system default and never enters the accessibility range.

Mapping scale tiers to iOS strategies

The Android scaleX ladder and iOS UIContentSizeCategory strategies meet at the same intent for each tier.

Scale tier Android iOS strategy Why they match
ScaleMax Decimal cap = unbounded default Both follow the user's setting with no ceiling, all the way through AX5.
Scale1 Decimal cap = 1.3× large · or largeToExcludeAccessibilityCategory for headers Both cap at the system default (Large). For Headers specifically, iOS also floors at Large via largeToExcludeAccessibilityCategory — the title never shrinks below default and never enters the AX range.
Scale0 Decimal cap = 1.0× (fixed) excludeAccessibilityCategory iOS has no true "freeze" strategy in the four named ones; excludeAccessibilityCategory is the closest match because the AX categories never reshape the layout. For genuinely fixed chrome (e.g. tab-bar labels that must never change size), use a non-UIFontMetrics-scaled font instead.
iOS content size category ladder, smallest to largest: xSmall · Small · Medium · Large (default) · xLarge · xxLarge · xxxLarge · AX1 · AX2 · AX3 · AX4 · AX5. AX1–AX5 only appear when the user enables "Larger Accessibility Sizes" in Settings.
Header rule. When a Header is implemented on iOS, prefer largeToExcludeAccessibilityCategory over plain large. The floor keeps the title from shrinking below the device default when the user's preferred size is below Large, which preserves the visual hierarchy headers depend on. TilesGrid and other layout-sensitive surfaces use excludeAccessibilityCategory for the same reason — the AX range would break the grid.
Scale0 has no exact iOS equivalent. The framework's Scale0 tier means "never grow" (1.0× fixed). The closest iOS strategy is excludeAccessibilityCategory, which still allows the user's preferred size from xSmall to xxxLarge to take effect — just not AX1–AX5. For true freeze (tab-bar labels, chrome that absolutely must not change size), use a fixed font that bypasses Dynamic Type rather than any of the four strategies.

Scaling Rules

Guidance

Workflow

Applying the framework #

Two decisions per component — the tier and the per-element reflow tokens. Everything in between is interpolated.

  1. Pick the tier for the component as a whole. Is it chrome (Scale0), navigation/container (Scale1), or user content (ScaleMax)?
  2. For Scale1 and ScaleMax, assign an extend token to each text element based on how much of it must remain readable at the cap.
  3. Assign virticalStack to the trailing column if it still clips after the extends are applied.
  4. The framework handles the rest. Intermediate sizes interpolate between the default layout and the cap layout you've configured. No per-step authoring required.
Scope

Applies to #

The framework is applied across the mobile component library — identical rules on iOS and Android.

ComponentTierNotes
Tab barScale0Anchored chrome — labels never scale.
HeadersScale1Title + subtitle pair stays inside the title region as text grows.
Search componentScale1Input field with placeholder; cap keeps the icon and field visible.
Input fields · Token fieldsScale1Form chrome — stays usable at cap.
BadgesScale1Including mention badges and counted labels.
Message composeScale1The compose chrome (icons + placeholder) stays anchored; the typed message body, when present, follows ScaleMax.
Chat list itemScaleMaxCanonical surface for the extend tokens — label, sublabel, and trailing date each carry their own extend value.
Threads list itemScaleMaxUses extend for the message body and virticalStack for the reply-count column when it clips.
