Scaling Rules

Architecture

Concept

Why a scaling framework #

Dynamic Type lets users push text to extreme sizes for accessibility. Without intervention, every text element scales freely — and components collapse: timestamps collide with labels, tab labels wrap to three lines, search placeholders shove their icons off-screen. The framework gives designers two levers — a per-component scale tier and per-element reflow tokens — so a chat row can stay legible at max zoom without breaking the rest of the screen.

Tune at the cap, not at every step. Designers configure behavior at one point — the upper bound of the component's scale tier. The framework interpolates every intermediate Dynamic Type size between the default layout and the configured max-zoom layout.

Monocore · Accessibility · Text & Icon contrast · June 2026
Accessibility — Text & Icon

Architecture

How to read this

Method #

For each role family, two side-by-side columns render the Text variant on the left and the Icon variant on the right. Each column carries the hex per mode, then a matrix of every opaque surface (rows) crossed with the four modes (columns), with the contrast ratio chipped:

4.5+ Text: AA Normal — Icon: well over threshold 3.0–4.49 Text: AA Large only (≥18pt or ≥14pt bold). Icon: still passes 3:1. <3.0 Fails both Text AA and non-text 3:1

Same chip thresholds for both columns. The colors map to the Text threshold (4.5/3.0) for consistency — that means an Icon cell showing an amber chip (3.0–4.49) is technically still passing its own 3:1 spec, but is visualized in amber so designers can compare Text and Icon at a glance. Icons fail only when the cell is red (<3.0).
Accent surface is single-purpose. Every text/icon role except On Accent fails on Surface/Accent. That's by design — the only valid pair on the accent surface is Text/On Accent or Icon/On Accent. The accent column in every matrix below shows that.
Disabled is intentionally below threshold. WCAG explicitly exempts inactive UI text. Disabled fails AA in every mode by design — that's the visual signal it's not interactive.
On this page
Method
Accessibility — Text & Icon · Architecture view
Accessibility

Stroke — WCAG non-text contrast

Every Stroke/* semantic role measured against every opaque Surface/* role in the two Theme modes. Strokes are evaluated against the WCAG 1.4.11 non-text-contrast threshold of 3:1 — but only roles that convey UI component boundaries are required to meet it. Decorative dividers and surface edges are not.

Roles
Monocore · Accessibility · Stroke contrast · June 2026
Accessibility — Stroke

Architecture

How to read this

Method #

For each stroke role, the matrix below shows its contrast ratio against every opaque surface in each of the four primary modes. Cells are chipped against the 3:1 non-text-contrast threshold.

3.0+ Meets WCAG 1.4.11 <3.0 Below threshold

Not every stroke needs 3:1. WCAG 1.4.11 applies to graphical elements that convey information — component boundaries that distinguish an interactive control from its background, focus rings, form-field outlines, etc. It does not apply to decorative separation. The Monocore stroke system has three tiers:
  • Stroke/Accessible — the AA-grade stroke. Used for focus rings, form field borders, and any boundary that must convey UI state. Required to meet 3:1 on every surface it can land on.
  • Stroke/Container (outer), Stroke/ContainerRaised — container edges. They define where a card or grouped region begins, but the contrast is also doing layout work, not state communication. Authoring with a target of 3:1 where reachable is preferred but not strictly required. Often paired with elevation or fill differentiation to reinforce boundaries.
  • Stroke/Divider, Stroke/Elevated (outside), Stroke/onMedia (outer) — decorative. Row dividers, hairline separators, and floating-surface edges that don't carry state information. Intentionally below 3:1 so they read as quiet visual organization. Not required to meet WCAG 1.4.11.
How to use this page. Look at the Stroke/Accessible matrix first — it should be all green; any red there is a real bug. For the other roles, red cells are expected; the matrix exists so designers can predict how a stroke will read against a specific surface, not to flag failures.
Note

Alpha strokes (Stroke/Elevated & Stroke/onMedia) #

Two strokes in the system now resolve to alpha values rather than solid greys — their effective color depends on whatever surface or image sits beneath them, so they cannot be evaluated with the foreground/background formula used in the matrix above. Treat both as decorative.

TokenLightDarkUsed for
Stroke/Elevated (outside) Black α5% White α24% The outside edge of floating and overlay surfaces — menus, popovers, sheets, callouts. Sits proud of the host surface as a hairline halo, not as a solid border.
Stroke/onMedia (outer) Black α7% White α13% Subtle outer edge on image thumbnails, avatars, and other media content. Because it's translucent, its effective color depends on the image beneath it.
On this page
Method Alpha strokes (Stroke/Elevated & Stroke/onMedia)
Accessibility — Stroke · Architecture view
Surface System

Elevation

Elevation is expressed by two Figma variable collections: Theme (Light - dark) holds the base semantic values, and Modal (Light - dark) is a formal Figma extension of Theme that overrides selected values for elevated contexts — sheets, drawers, popovers, modal flows. Each collection carries just two modes: Light and Dark. When a designer binds a modal frame to the Modal extension, every non-overridden token still resolves through Theme (so brand changes cascade automatically), while the 30 elevated tokens resolve to their Modal-specific values. This page lists which tokens are overridden and why.

30 roles overridden in Modal 247 roles total in Theme Modal is a Figma extension of Theme

Modal overrides by category #

Surface roles overridden in Modal

9 of 34 Surface roles carry Modal overrides. These are the elevation-critical surfaces — Canvas, Sunken, Interactive, RaisedSecondary, Floating, Quaternary, Glass Single, Group/Primary/Base. Overrides typically bump one Grey step to preserve lift above the Overlay canvas.

Elevation

Guidance

Architectural rule

Overlay surfaces and the Modal extension #

The Modal extension exists because content rendered inside an Overlay needs different values than content on the base canvas. The rule below explains why — and what breaks if a modal frame is left bound to Theme instead of Modal.

Overlay surfaces in dark mode are the L2 canvas. Modal/sheet content must be set to L2 mode.

Set the frame mode to Dark L2 for any content nested inside an Surface/Overlay, Surface/Floating, or other temporary elevated surface. If you leave it on Dark L1, surfaces that should lift above the overlay will instead match it — in the worst case, the card becomes mathematically identical to its background and vanishes.

Frame mode: Dark L1 wrong Container vs Overlay: 1.00:1
Stack: Canvas #000000 → Overlay #1a1a1a → Container #1a1a1a
Frame mode: Dark L2 correct Container vs Overlay: 1.06:1 · 2 Grey steps
Stack: Canvas #1a1a1a → Overlay #1a1a1a → Container #1f1f1f
  • The architectural contract. Surface/Overlay in Dark resolves to #1a1a1a (Grey/10) — which is also Surface/Canvas in Dark L2. Overlay is the L2 canvas at the surface layer. Setting the inside-overlay frame to L2 makes every nested role re-resolve correctly against that elevated canvas.
  • Symptoms if you forget. Surface/RaisedBase and Surface/RaisedSecondary drop from 1.66:1 to 1.38:1 against the Overlay (17% less lift). Surface/Group/Primary/Base becomes mathematically identical to the Overlay (1.00:1) and disappears entirely.
  • What gets fixed by L2. Canvas L2 = Overlay (no visible delta needed at that layer). Containers/Primary/Base steps Grey/10 → Grey/12. RaisedSecondary stays Grey/20 but the perceptual delta to the now-matching Overlay/Canvas pair is consistent. The hierarchy holds.
  • Light mode is fine. Canvas and Overlay are both #ffffff in both light tiers, so the relationships hold mathematically without needing an L2 mode shift. Card delineation against a white overlay relies on stroke + shadow (the same way it does on the white canvas), not on a tonal step.

Stroke/Container (outer) preserves badge silhouettes when fill matches the container surface.

The real iOS Badge component fills its pill with Surface/RaisedSecondary and outlines it with Stroke/Container (outer). When that badge sits inside Surface/Group/Primary/Container — the standard iOS list cell — the badge fill resolves to the same hex as the container surface in both light and dark. Without the stroke, the pill has zero tonal lift and disappears.

Badge fill alone no stroke Fill 1.00:1 against Container
Stack: Canvas #1a1a1a → Overlay #1a1a1a → Container #333333 → Badge fill #333333 (no boundary)
Badge fill + Stroke/Container (outer) correct Edge ratio 1.51:1 — silhouette holds
Stack: Canvas #1a1a1a → Overlay #1a1a1a → Container #333333 → Badge fill #333333 + stroke #4d4d4d
  • Same hex on both sides. Surface/RaisedSecondary and Surface/Group/Primary/Container resolve to #f0f0f0 in light themes and #333333 in dark. A badge filled with one inside the other has 1.00:1 contrast at the fill layer in both modes. Without an edge token, the pill silhouette doesn't exist.
  • What Stroke/Container (outer) contributes. Grey/90 (#e6e6e6) in light, Grey/16 (#292929) in dark — both clear the WCAG 1.4.11 3:1 threshold against every standard container surface. On the badge specifically, the 1px stroke draws the boundary the matching fill can't.
  • Where the badge actually uses it. The Static and Interactive Badge variants in CXD-iOS bind their container stroke to Stroke/Container (outer) by default (with Stroke/Default as the previous behaviour migrated away from). Confirmed against node 83392:62611: fill Surface/RaisedSecondary, stroke Stroke/Container (outer), label Text/Secondary, avatar border Surface/Dominant.

Elevation · Guidance view
Elevation

Architecture

Concept

Two collections, one extension relationship #

The old system expressed elevation as an L1/L2 mode inside a single Color collection — every variable carried four mode values (Light L1, Dark L1, Light L2, Dark L2). That's been replaced with a two-collection model: Theme (Light - dark) holds the base values with just Light and Dark modes; Modal (Light - dark) is a formal Figma extension (created via the "Extend collection" action in the Variables panel) that inherits every variable from Theme and only stores overrides for the 30 tokens that need to shift in an elevated context.

Modal overrides Theme — it doesn't duplicate it. When you bind a frame to Modal, every token that isn't explicitly overridden falls through to its Theme value, so brand refreshes, primitive swaps, and general theme changes cascade automatically. Only the 30 elevated overrides are stored in Modal; the other 217 variables are pure inheritance.

Below, each category lists only the roles that are overridden in Modal. For every overridden role, the swatches show Theme's base value alongside Modal's override, so the elevation delta is obvious. A short rationale explains what perceptual relationship the override is preserving.

Reading the swatch rows. Each role shows swatches for the Theme (Light and Dark) base values and the Modal (Light and Dark) overrides. The theme-side swatches represent the app default; the modal-side represent what renders inside a sheet, drawer, popover, or modal flow that has been bound to the Modal extension.
Pattern

Nested elevation in an iOS sheet #

The contact-card sheet below combines four surface tokens at three depths. It's the canonical proof of why Surface/RaisedPrimary exists alongside Surface/RaisedSecondary: pills and tiles sit directly on the sheet body, while badges nested inside a list container need one more Grey step of lift to read above the cell. Tokens are read directly from the CXD-iOS Sheet binding.

Hover a pulsing dot to see the surface token + resolved hex for that region.
Image not found Save the iOS sheet screenshot as images/sheet-nested-elevation.png in the docs folder. Expected dimensions: 2x retina screenshots of the iOS contact-card sheet, light + dark side by side.

Layer stack — bottom to top

  1. Surface/Canvas #ffffff · L ↔ #000000 · D The screen behind the sheet. The avatar floats here above the sheet's top edge.
  2. Surface/Group/Primary/Base #ffffff · L ↔ #1a1a1a · D The sheet body. The CXD-iOS Sheet instance binds its outer fill to this token, not Surface/Overlay — the sheet is the app's container, not a system overlay.
  3. Surface/RaisedSecondary #f0f0f0 · L ↔ #333333 · D Sits directly on the sheet body. Used for the pill labels and the action tiles (Chat, People, Share, Views, Copilot). One Grey step above the sheet is enough to feel tappable.
  4. Surface/Group/Primary/Container #f0f0f0 · L ↔ #333333 · D The grouped list cell holding "Spatial Annotations", "Background effects", and "Call my phone". Same tonal step as RaisedSecondary; the two roles are parallel "one-step-above-sheet" tokens for different intents (chip vs. grouped container).
  5. Surface/RaisedPrimary #e0e0e0 · L ↔ #3d3d3d · D The reason RaisedPrimary exists. The "Badge" pill sits inside the list container. If it used RaisedSecondary, its fill would equal the container's fill exactly — it would disappear. RaisedPrimary is one Grey step higher (Grey/88 in light, Grey/24 in dark) so it lifts cleanly without needing a stroke.
LayerTokenLight L1Dark L1Step from parent
Sheet bodySurface/Group/Primary/Base#ffffff (Grey/100)#1a1a1a (Grey/10)0 (L) · +10 (D)
Pills + buttonsSurface/RaisedSecondary#f0f0f0 (Grey/94)#333333 (Grey/20)−6 (L) · +10 (D)
List containerSurface/Group/Primary/Container#f0f0f0 (Grey/94)#333333 (Grey/20)same step as RaisedSecondary
Badge inside listSurface/RaisedPrimary#e0e0e0 (Grey/88)#3d3d3d (Grey/24)−6 (L) · +4 (D)
The choice rule for nested surfaces. When picking a surface for an element that sits inside an already-elevated container, count the Grey distance from the host surface to the available Raised tokens. If the next-step-up (RaisedSecondary) collides with the host, skip it and use RaisedPrimary — that's the whole reason there are two parallel Raised tokens instead of one.
The stroke alternative. The CXD-iOS Badge component binds to Surface/RaisedSecondary + Stroke/Container (outer). That's a deliberate trade-off — one fill primitive across every badge context with the stroke handling the boundary. In patterns where designers want tonal lift instead of an outline, swap the Badge container fill to Surface/RaisedPrimary and drop the stroke. Both approaches pass the surface system contract.

277 tokens compared across Windows Fluent, Android Fluent, and the CXD-Variables Figma library. Windows mapping

Guidance

Next steps

Migration priorities #

The audit isn't a plan on its own — it's the raw material for one. Three planning axes fall out of the data:

  1. Resolve the 19 hard mismatches first. The N rows are tokens where the same design intent resolves to different hex values on Windows and Android. Each one is either a bug (should be unified) or an intentional platform divergence (should be documented as such). Both outcomes require a decision.
  2. Fill in the in_figma_variables column. The 214 Unknown rows can be reconciled against CXD-Variables by intent. Once complete, the audit becomes a bridge table — every intent has either a Figma variable name or an explicit "not migrated yet" flag.
  3. Enumerate hardcoded uses. The hardcoded_uses column is currently 0 across the board. Populating it with actual occurrence counts (from a codebase scan) turns the audit into a prioritization tool — the intents with the most hardcoded uses become the highest-impact migration wins.

Architecture

Method

What's in this audit #

Each row is a single design intent (e.g. "background/surface", "text/primary", "border/interactive") paired with the token that expresses it in each platform. The values_match column reports whether the light and dark values are numerically identical across Windows and Android. The in_figma_variables column reports whether that intent is already represented in the CXD-Variables library. The audit doesn't attempt to unify tokens on its own — it produces the delta list that migration work is planned against.

At a glance

277

6
Values match (Y)
19
Values differ (N)
4
Partial match

The remaining 248 rows are either "—" (only exists in one platform, so there's nothing to compare) or blank. The high dash count reflects that most tokens in Windows and Android don't have a one-to-one twin on the other platform — the migration work is largely about deciding whether to bridge them.

How to read values_match. Y means the Windows and Android hex values are identical in both light and dark. N means they differ — a real cross-platform drift that migration needs to resolve. Partial means they match in one theme but not the other. — means the intent only has a token on one of the two platforms, so there's nothing to compare.
How to read in_figma_variables. The current audit uses Unknown as a default for rows that haven't been reconciled with CXD-Variables yet. Reconciling this column is the next planned pass — the tool's data model already supports the values Yes, No, and specific figma variable names, so it can be filled in as each intent gets mapped.

Monocore

Architecture

How the Teams UI upgrade became Monocore: what feeds the design system, how it adapts per OS, and why one system ships under two code-library names.

2 platforms 2 code libraries Updated October 2026
System

One design system, two names #

This page describes the relationship between Teams, SharePoint and Engage and a shared design system. This system is realized in separate code libraries but shares tokens and typography to enable smooth integrations within Teams as a host app.

Naming

Two code libraries, one design system #

This is the part that causes confusion, so it is stated plainly. The word Monocore does two jobs.

Teams Mobile
Teams UI

The code library keeps its existing name inside the Teams codebase. It receives new visual-refresh tokens and the OS-native concepts combine into a major update for the design system. In Teams, “Monocore” describes the upgrade.

SharePoint & Engage
Monocore

The SharePoint and Engage team consumes the same design system through a separate and shared code library, which retains the name “Monocore” since no existing library exists.

When someone says “Monocore”, they mean the design system unless they are a SharePoint or Engage engineer talking about an import. Both libraries build from the identical Figma source; neither is “more Monocore” than the other.
Platforms

Per-OS adaptation #

The design system is a single source of truth, but it does not render identically on both platforms. Each OS has native idioms that get baked into components, and the two are not symmetric. The differences below are taken directly from Apple's Human Interface Guidelines and Google's Material 3 documentation.

Devices. iOS covers iPhone and iPad (e.g. iPhone 17, iPad Pro); Android covers phones, foldables and tablets across many OEMs (e.g. Pixel 10, Galaxy Z Fold).

iOS 26 Apple Human Interface Guidelines
  • Materials. Liquid Glass "forms a distinct functional layer for controls and navigation elements — like tab bars and sidebars — that floats above the content layer." It is reserved for that layer: "Don't use Liquid Glass in the content layer."
  • Material variants. Two: Regular "blurs and adjusts the luminosity of background content to maintain legibility" and is what "most system components use"; Clear is "highly translucent" and only for "components that appear over visually rich backgrounds." Content-layer surfaces use the four standard materials: ultra-thin, thin, regular, thick.
  • Elevation. Depth is expressed through translucency and blur, with "scroll edge effects" that blur and fade content as it passes beneath a bar.
  • Typography. SF Pro is the system font. Default body size is 17 pt, minimum 11 pt. Eleven text styles (Large Title 34 → Caption 2 11) scale through Dynamic Type from xSmall to AX5; "avoid light font weights."
  • Navigation. "A tab bar floats above content at the bottom of the screen" on a Liquid Glass background. On iPad it moves: "the system displays a tab bar near the top of the screen," convertible to a sidebar.
  • Adaptivity. Size-class driven. Layout must "adapt seamlessly to appearance changes — like device orientation, Dark Mode, and Dynamic Type," and "reduce the number of columns when the font size increases."
Android · Material 3 Material Design 3 documentation
  • Surfaces. No translucent navigation layer. Material 3 "represents elevation mainly using tonal color overlays," and "the overlay color comes from the primary color slot." Surfaces are opaque tonal steps, not glass.
  • Surface roles. A single expanded colour system — "surface, surface-variant and background alongside on-surface, on-surface-variant" — built from "five key colors," each with "a tonal palette of 13 tones." There is no Regular / Clear split.
  • Elevation. Tonal first, shadow second: "increasing tonal elevation uses a more prominent tone — in addition to shadows." Exposed as separate tonalElevation and shadowElevation.
  • Typography. Roboto is the default. A 15-role scale — display, headline, title, body, label × large / medium / small — e.g. bodyLarge 16/24, labelSmall 11/16, in sp. "Display Small can be assigned different values depending upon the device context, such as a phone or a tablet."
  • Navigation. A navigation bar holds "three to five destinations of equal importance" and is for "compact window sizes." It is anchored, not floating, and does not relocate on larger screens — larger windows use a rail or drawer instead.
  • Adaptivity. Window-size-class driven, with fixed dp breakpoints: compact < 600, medium 600–840, expanded 840–1200, large 1200–1600, extra-large ≥ 1600. "The window size class can change throughout the lifetime of your app."
Why this is asymmetric. iOS organises depth around a translucent navigation layer; Material 3 organises it around opaque tonal steps. A Monocore component therefore cannot be a 1:1 port — the iOS header carries Liquid Glass, the Android header carries a tonal surface, and the shared tokens sit beneath both.

Sources. HIG · Materials · HIG · Typography · HIG · Tab bars · HIG · Designing for iOS · M3 · Material Design 3 in Compose · M3 · Navigation bar · M3 · Window size classes

Monocore

Teams information architecture

How a Teams mobile screen is assembled in Monocore iOS: a Shell or Sheet supplies the chrome, a Canvas supplies the content, and the Canvas inventory maps one-to-one onto the Teams app's tabs. SharePoint and Engage get their own IA pages; the Shell and Sheet layer below is shared by every app on a device.

Teams 2 shared containers 33 canvases Updated October 2026
Containers

Shell, Sheet and Canvas #

The container layer is per device, not per app: Teams, SharePoint and Engage on iOS all mount their screens in the same Shell Template and Sheet, and only the Canvas layer is app-specific. Every screen in the Teams POR file is built from the same three layers. A Canvas is a 402-wide, chrome-less screen body: no status bar, no header, no tab bar. The chrome comes from one of two containers. The Shell Template wraps the root view of each bottom tab. The Sheet - Full Screen wraps anything pushed or presented on top of a tab, and itself hosts a Shell so the header and keyboard behave the same way at every level.

Container
Shell Template

Status bar, header toolbar, content slot and the five-item tab bar. Wraps the root view of each tab and is also what a Sheet hosts, so a pushed screen's header is the same component as a tab's.

Container
Sheet - Full Screen - iPhone

Header slot, content slot and an optional keyboard. Six size variants (Secondary, Dominant, Stacked, 2/3, 1/3, 1/3 Secondary) cover pushed screens, modals and partial sheets.

Content
Canvas - …

One per screen. Built almost entirely from the list system: Grouped list → Generic List rows, Section Header, Description list, Accessories; conversation rows use Timer / Thread List-item; Calendar uses Agenda list.

Inventory

Canvas inventory by Teams tab #

Canvases are grouped by the Teams tab that hosts them.

  • Default app bar: Activity, Chat, Teams, Calendar. Calls and Files sit behind More on mobile.
  • Search lives inside each tab's header.
  • Me menu holds status, out-of-office, notifications and Settings.
  • Level is where the canvas sits in that tree: L1 tab root inside a Shell, L2 pushed or modal inside a Sheet.

Reading the table. Everything in the Chat, Teams, More and Me groups bottoms out in the same five list primitives (Grouped list, Generic List - Primary, Section Header, Description list, Accessories), so a Code Connect map of those five covers most of the app. The six canvases marked "none" exist as components but no documentation board places them yet.
Dev notes

Dev notes #

Data
Where this comes from

Derived from the Teams POR page of Monocore-iOS: 33 Canvas components, ~170 instances, every one wrapped by either Shell Template (tab roots) or Sheet - Full Screen - iPhone → Shell Template (pushed and modal screens). The two iPad instances use Modal - Full Screen - iPad.

Rule
The rule

A Canvas never carries chrome; a container never carries content. Canvas variants encode view state (Dashboard.Type, Settings.Page, Me menu.Level × Screen). The container it sits in encodes navigation level. iPad reuses the same canvases inside Modal - Full Screen - iPad.

Sources. Canvas, container and instance data from the Teams POR page of Monocore-iOS (21 October 2026). Teams app structure from Microsoft Support · Getting to know Microsoft Teams (Free) (Chat, Communities, Meet, Activity tabs; search inside tabs; profile menu → Settings), TeachUcomp · The Teams interface overview ("the buttons in the app bar are Activity, Chat, Teams, Calendar, Calls, and Files") and University of Greenwich · Teams menus and navigation (mobile hamburger/profile menu: status, out of office, notifications, settings).

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Dev notes

How this page is parsed from Figma #

Each artboard is an instance of New component: a Content block with Title Block=Page Title, then a vertical Slot. Inside the slot, a Content block with Title Block=Section primary starts a section, and each Slot block is one example: its Content block (Section primary light) carries the title and an optional caption, and its PASTE HERE slot (the name may carry a suffix such as PASTE HERE5) holds the component instance(s) whose variant properties become the monospace line under the preview.

Regeneration rule. Take the artboards on the page in canvas order (left to right). For each one, walk its slot in order; emit an h1 for the page title, an h2 for every Section primary block, and a card for every Slot block. Export each instance in PASTE HERE as SVG when it is pure vector (icons, Presence, Cutout, the icon Avatars) and as a 2× PNG, or an SVG with the photo embedded, when it contains an image fill. Nothing on this page is hand-authored except the header copy.

Dev notes

How this page is parsed from Figma #

Each artboard is an instance of New component: a Content block with Title Block=Page Title, then a vertical Slot. Inside the slot, a Content block with Title Block=Section primary starts a section, and each Slot block is one example: its Content block (Section primary light) carries the title and an optional caption, and its PASTE HERE slot holds the component instance(s) whose variant properties become the monospace line under the preview.

Regeneration rule. Take the artboards on the page in canvas order (left to right). For each one, walk its slot in order; emit an h1 for the page title, an h2 for every Section primary block, and a card for every Slot block. Each placeholder carries the instance's node id in data-figma-id and its size, so the export pass replaces it with an <img> (SVG for pure vector, 2× PNG with alpha when the component uses a photo or a blur material) without re-parsing the artboard.

Figma page Card; nodes: Card 106947:206801.

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Figma page Images; nodes: Image and Grid 106947:215251.

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Dev notes

How this page is parsed from Figma #

Each artboard is an instance of New component: a Content block with Title Block=Page Title, then a vertical Slot. Inside the slot, a Content block with Title Block=Section primary starts a section, and each Slot block is one example: its Content block (Section primary light) carries the title and an optional caption, and its PASTE HERE slot holds the component instance(s) whose variant properties become the monospace line under the preview.

Regeneration rule. Take the artboards on the page in canvas order (left to right). For each one, walk its slot in order; emit an h1 for the page title, an h2 for every Section primary block, and a card for every Slot block. Each placeholder carries the instance's node id in data-figma-id and its size, so the export pass replaces it with an <img> (SVG for pure vector, 2× PNG with alpha when the component uses a photo or a blur material) without re-parsing the artboard.

Dev notes

How this page is parsed from Figma #

Each artboard is an instance of New component: a Content block with Title Block=Page Title, then a vertical Slot. Inside the slot, a Content block with Title Block=Section primary starts a section, and each Slot block is one example: its Content block (Section primary light) carries the title and an optional caption, and its PASTE HERE slot holds the component instance(s) whose variant properties become the monospace line under the preview.

Regeneration rule. Take the artboards on the page in canvas order (left to right). For each one, walk its slot in order; emit an h1 for the page title, an h2 for every Section primary block, and a card for every Slot block. Each placeholder carries the instance's node id in data-figma-id and its size, so the export pass replaces it with an <img> (SVG for pure vector, 2× PNG with alpha when the component uses a photo or a blur material) without re-parsing the artboard.

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Figma page Tabbars; nodes: Tab bar 106947:228767.

Synthetic card

Rendered from the documentation artboard on the Synthetic Card page of Monocore iOS. Each artboard is a vertical flow of titled blocks holding one or more component variants; this page keeps that order and naming so it can be regenerated when the artboards change.

1 Figma artboard 1 blocks Read 1 Nov 2026

Synthetic card #

Variant

Default
Syntheric Card
Dev notes

How this page is parsed from Figma #

Each artboard is an instance of New component: a Content block with Title Block=Page Title, then a vertical Slot. Inside the slot, a Content block with Title Block=Section primary starts a section, and each Slot block is one example: its Content block (Section primary light) carries the title and an optional caption, and its PASTE HERE slot holds the component instance(s) whose variant properties become the monospace line under the preview.

Regeneration rule. Take the artboards on the page in canvas order (left to right). For each one, walk its slot in order; emit an h1 for the page title, an h2 for every Section primary block, and a card for every Slot block. Each placeholder carries the instance's node id in data-figma-id and its size, so the export pass replaces it with an <img> (SVG for pure vector, 2× PNG with alpha when the component uses a photo or a blur material) without re-parsing the artboard.

Figma page Synthetic Card; nodes: Synthetic card 106947:212439.

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Accessibility

Accessibility #

The published component carries a documentation link to the Teams Mobile A11y guidance; the notes below are the parts that bind at spec time.

  • Target size. Only Large (52dp) clears a 44dp minimum on its own. Medium (40dp) and Small (28dp) need the host surface to extend the hit area — the visual box is not the target.
  • Icon-only buttons. Turning Show label off removes the accessible name with it. Supply one explicitly; never ship an icon-only Button without it.
  • Disabled contrast. Text/Disabled on Surface/Disabled is deliberately below the text contrast floor, which is permitted for disabled controls — but it means disabled state must never be the only signal that an action is unavailable.
  • Press feedback. See the Accent Pressed note above: until that binding is fixed, Accent buttons need a non-colour press affordance.

Button Component

Architecture

Why Monocore ships two button components instead of one, what each axis is actually responsible for, and the exact layer tree behind both.

Model

The Configuration Model #

The Button separates three concerns, and deliberately refuses to absorb a fourth.

Style is the emphasis axis — how loudly the action asks to be taken. Size is the density axis — how much room the host surface affords. State is the interaction axis — Rest, Pressed, Disabled. All three are orthogonal, so 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 variants publish with no exclusions: there is no combination of emphasis, density and interaction that is meaningless.

The fourth concern — width behaviour — is what Button Full-width exists to hold. It could have been a boolean on the main set, and that is the tempting design; it was split out because full-width buttons only ever occur at Large, and folding them in would have published 27 unreachable Medium and Small full-width variants to gain one property.

Width is a container decision, not a button decision. The standard Button hugs its label at every size. Anything that needs to fill its container is a different component with different responsive rules — portrait fills the width inside 16dp padding, landscape and tablet cap at 340dp.
Structure

Figma Anatomy #

The exact layer tree of both published components — the map for translating Figma structure to code. Purple entries are slots (swap targets that become SLOT properties at compile time). Blue entries are bound text properties. Items marked optional are toggled per instance.

Button83361-7413 · 27 variants
Button (Style × Size × State · hugs content · radius: pill, or 24/8/4 for Subtle) └─ Content (row, centred · padding-y 0 · height 52 / 40 / 28) ├─ [slot] Slot (20×20 box, 16×16 glyph · 16×16 box, 12×12 glyph at Small) — optional, on by default ├─ [text] Label — optional (Show label) · iOS/Button 1, or iOS/Button 2 at Small └─ [slot] Icon (same box sizes as Slot) — optional, off by default
Button Full-width83865-65664 · 9 variants
Button Full-width (Style × State · 393×52 as published · radius pill) └─ Content (row, centred · height 24 · padding 20 × 14 · gap 8) ├─ [slot] Slot (20×20 box, 16×16 glyph) — optional, on by default └─ [text] Label — iOS/Button 1

Properties & Slots

Beyond the three variant axes, each instance exposes four instance properties. Icon slots are swap targets; the label is a bound text property.

PropertyTypeDefaultNotes
Slot (left icon)Instance swapOn20×20 box / 16×16 glyph at Large & Medium; 16×16 box / 12×12 glyph at Small
LabelTextButtonTruncates with ellipsis; single line, never wraps
Show labelBooleanOnOff yields an icon-only button — pair with an accessible name
Right iconBoolean + swapOffTrailing affordance (chevron, caret) — hidden by default in every variant
The label owns the width. The Button has no fixed width at any size — it hugs its content, and horizontal padding is the only lever. If you need a fixed or edge-to-edge footprint, that is what Button Full-width is for; do not stretch the standard Button.
One row, three children, no wrappers. Unlike the Card, the Button has no nested containers — the variant does all the work and Content is a single auto-layout row. That is why the whole set fits in 27 variants: there is no internal structure for a variant to reconfigure.
Structure

How Size Is Expressed #

Size does not scale the button — it re-selects four independent values.

Height is set explicitly on Content (52 / 40 / 28) with vertical padding pinned at 0, so the row centres its children rather than growing from them. Horizontal padding, gap, icon box and type style are each chosen per size and do not interpolate: 16 / 10 / 8–10 padding, 8 / 8 / 4 gap, 20 / 20 / 16 icon box, Button 1 / Button 1 / Button 2 type.

Note the pattern: Large and Medium are the same button at two heights — identical gap, icon box and type style, differing only in height and horizontal padding. Small is the real break, dropping to a 16dp icon box and the Button 2 ramp. If you are implementing a size scale in code, model it as two tiers with a height variable, not three arbitrary sets.

Known issues

Published Debt #

Three things in the published set are inconsistent. They are documented here so implementers reproduce them knowingly — or fix them at the source rather than in each consumer.

IssueWhereEffect
Accent Pressed binds a different token that resolves to the same colour as RestAccent · all sizesNo visible press feedback on the highest-emphasis button
“Outline accent” publishes border width 0 at Large and MediumOutline accent · L, MFilled grey, not outlined; only Small carries the 0.5dp stroke
Subtle changes corner radius between Rest (24) and Pressed / Disabled (8, or 4 at Small)Subtle · all sizesLatent — invisible while Subtle has no fill, wrong the moment one is added
Do not normalise these silently in code. A consumer that quietly fixes the radius or adds a press tint puts the implementation out of sync with the library, and the next Figma pull will look like a regression. Raise them against the component set.

Accessibility

Accessibility #

  • Never put an action in a call out. The component has no interactive slot and no dismiss control — anything essential inside it is unreachable by keyboard or switch control. It is for hints, not decisions.
  • Announce it when it appears. A call out that fades in unannounced is invisible to a screen reader user. Tie it to its anchor and announce it politely on show.
  • Don't rely on hover or a timeout. On touch there is no hover, and an auto-dismissing hint punishes anyone reading slowly. Give the user a way to dismiss it and don't gate anything behind having read it.
  • 248dp is a hard ceiling. Long strings wrap rather than widen, and at large accessibility text sizes a two-line hint becomes five. Keep the copy short enough to survive that.

Call Out Component

Architecture

Why an eight-value axis is the right shape for a tooltip, what the component deliberately refuses to own, and where the published set drifts.

Model

The Configuration Model #

One axis, eight values, and a hard boundary around what the component will not do.

Tip location is the only property. It sets two things at once: which edge the tail emerges from, and how the body aligns against that tail. Those two are inseparable — a tip on the bottom-left edge only makes sense with the body's left edge aligned to it — which is why they are one variant rather than two axes that could be combined into nonsense.

What the component does not own is placement. It has no anchor reference, no offset property and no collision behaviour. It is a shape that points in a direction; deciding which direction, and where on screen to put it, is the host's job. That is a deliberate split: anchoring depends on scroll position, safe areas and keyboard state, none of which a Figma variant can model.

Choosing the variant is the flip logic. When a call out would run off the top of the screen, the host doesn't ask the component to adapt — it swaps Bottom center for Top center. The eight variants exist precisely so that flipping is a variant change and never a layout hack.
Structure

Figma Anatomy #

Two children in a single flex line. Their order is what encodes the tip's edge — there is no positioning trick underneath.

Call Out83507-103793 · 8 variants
Call Out (Tip location · drop shadow: Shadows/Light/Shadow 16) ├─ Container (fill Brand/Accent Dominant · radius 8 · padding 8 · gap 8 │ min 80×56 · max-width 248 · clips content) │ └─ [text] Body — iOS/Subhead 2, Text/On Accent, wraps at 248 └─ Tip (62×7 for top/bottom · 7×14 for left/right) Order per variant Bottom * Container → Tip — tail below the body Top * Tip → Container — tail above, mirrored vertically Left * Tip → Container — tail leading Right * Container → Tip — tail trailing, mirrored horizontally
The tip is an asset, not a drawn shape. Both tip geometries ship as flat SVGs with the fill baked in rather than as vector layers bound to Brand/Accent Dominant. Re-theming the container will not re-theme the tail — in code, draw the tip from the same token as the container so the two can never drift apart.
Content

One Slot, and Why #

The Container has a bound text property and nothing else — no icon slot, no action slot, no close button.

That is a scope decision, not an oversight. A tooltip with a button becomes a coach mark, which needs focus management, a dismissal contract and a way to be re-summoned. Adding an action slot here would let any surface create an unreachable control inside a transient popup. The 8dp internal gap hints that a second child was once anticipated; today it never has one.

If you need an action, you need a different component. Do not slot a Button into a Call Out instance. Raise the need for a coach-mark component instead — the accessibility contract is genuinely different.
Known issues

Published Debt #

IssueWhereEffect
Min height is 44dp instead of 56dpTop left onlyOne variant sits 12dp shorter than its seven siblings with the same copy
Tip is a baked SVG asset with a hard-coded fillAll 8 variantsContainer and tail can drift apart under re-theming; dark theme is not expressible
The tip asset is a 62dp frame holding a ~14dp tailTop / bottom variantsThe tail is centred in mostly-transparent padding, so its offset from the body edge is locked at ~31dp however wide the call out is — a corner-anchored tip is not expressible
No Left top / Right bottom corner variantsSide tipsSide-anchored call outs on tall elements have no correct alignment
Internal gap of 8dp with only one childContainerHarmless today; signals an intended second slot that was never published
The 44dp outlier is the cheap fix. It is a single value on a single variant and almost certainly unintentional — worth correcting at the source before any implementation encodes two different minimum heights.

Usage Examples #

Accessibility

Accessibility #

  • The card is one target, the icons are others. Base and File chiclets carry a trailing slot, and File carries two. Nesting interactive glyphs inside an interactive card needs explicit, separate accessible names — otherwise a screen reader announces one blob with three actions.
  • Attribution is 11dp on 11dp line height. Caption 2 is the smallest type in the system and it is set solid, with no leading. It will clip at large accessibility text sizes; treat the attribution as content that must reflow, not as a fixed-height row.
  • The quote bar is decorative. On Reply and Forward it carries no accessible meaning — the relationship must be in the announced text (“replying to Charlotte D.”), not in a 4dp grey rule.
  • Overlay buttons sit on arbitrary media. The scrim (78% opaque #292929) is what makes the glyph legible, not the image behind it. Never drop the scrim to let more of the thumbnail through.
  • Dismiss only appears on the compose box. When a chiclet is dismissible, the control is 20dp — well under a 44dp target. The host must extend the hit area.

Chiclet · Spec · Monocore · November 2026
Chiclet Component

Architecture

One shell, six interiors, and a family that has outgrown its name. What Layout actually switches, why the grid is sparse, and what needs consolidating.

Model

The Configuration Model #

Chiclet is the one component in this set where the variant axis changes structure, not just style.

Button varies colour and size. Divider varies an inset. Chiclet's Layout axis swaps the entire interior: Base is an icon-text-chevron row, Reply prepends a quote bar and an attribution glyph, File Chiclet leads with a filetype icon and trails a pair of actions, Video is a media plate with a centred play control and no text at all. Only the shell — 265dp wide, 16dp radius, Surface/Primary, a one-pixel border — survives across all seven.

That is defensible because the thing a chiclet represents is what changes, and the representation dictates the anatomy. It is also why the axis cannot be decomposed: there is no meaningful “Reply + File”.

The shell is the contract, not the interior. Anything consuming a chiclet can rely on the 265dp width, the 16dp radius and the border treatment. Nothing else is stable across layouts — so never write host code that reaches into a chiclet expecting a particular child.
Model

Why the Grid Is Sparse #

Six layouts × two Image values would be twelve variants. Seven are published, and the five gaps split into two different reasons.

Four gaps are meaningless combinations. Base, Base + actions, Reply and Forward have no media plate to switch on, so Image=True would render identically to False. Publishing them would be four variants of pure noise.

One gap is a missing state. Video / Image=False is absent because a video chiclet with no thumbnail has nothing to show — but that is exactly the state a real client hits while the thumbnail is still loading or has failed. Today there is no published answer for it.

Meanwhile Reply and Forward do carry media, through a separate boolean that reveals a 40×40 thumbnail. Two mechanisms for the same idea, on the same component, is the structural problem underneath the naming collision.

Unify the two media mechanisms before adding anything else. Either the Image axis covers every layout that can show media, or media is always a boolean-revealed slot. Keeping both guarantees the next contributor picks the wrong one.

Video is the only layout with no text. It publishes no title, body or attribution — the whole card is a media plate with one control. Any caption you see next to a video in product is the host's, not the chiclet's.

Published Debt #

IssueWhereEffect
Two published sets are both named “Chiclet”83310-17383 and 106838-39902Library search cannot distinguish the message chiclet from the live-meeting bar
A loose component is slash-named Chiclet/Live meeting (Dominant)/False84263-9937Displays as if it were a variant of a set it does not belong to
Two unrelated properties both express “image”Whole setGenerated code has to name them image and image1; authors pick the wrong one
Filename type style changes between File variantsFile Chiclet, Image False vs TrueBody 2 at 15dp becomes Button 2 at 13dp for identical content
No Video / Image=FalseVideoNo published state for a missing or still-loading thumbnail
Media height of 171.568dpFile Chiclet, Image=TrueA fractional value baked from a ratio; will not survive a redraw cleanly
Fix the names before the values. The duplicate set name and the slash-named orphan are cheap to correct and are actively misleading anyone searching the library. The typography and media-mechanism issues are real but at least discoverable once you are looking at the right component.

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Figma page Compose; nodes: Compose keyboard 106947:228708.

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Figma page Content Card; nodes: Content card 106947:213408.

Usage Examples #

Content Card is a reference to one thing with at most one action zone.

Link preview in a message
Quarterly review deckcontoso.sharepoint.com

If it needs more than one region, it is a Card. Multiple content areas, dividers or a button group belong to the Card; a quoted or forwarded message is a Chiclet.
Accessibility

Accessibility #

  • The card is one target; the right accessory is another. A chevron that navigates and a card that opens must be separately named, or announced as one combined action — never two unlabeled taps.
  • Both selection affordances can be on at once. L-Checkbox and Radio are independent booleans on the same leading slot; only one should ever be enabled, chosen by the list's selection model.
  • Titles truncate on one line. The ellipsis is visual only — keep the full title in the accessible name.
  • Media is decorative by default. A 64dp thumbnail rarely adds information the title lacks; expose it as decorative unless it is the content (a photo message).

Accessibility

Accessibility #

  • A plain Divider is decorative. It carries no information a screen reader needs; expose it as decorative rather than as a separator with a role, so it does not add noise to a long list.
  • Section Divider is not decorative. Its centre content — a label like “Unread”, or a button — is real content and must be reachable. Do not hide the whole component.
  • The rule fails text contrast by design. Stroke/Divider (#e0e0e0) against a white surface is a non-text boundary, which is permitted — but it means a divider can never be the only cue that two things are different. Grouping, spacing and headings carry the meaning.
  • Do not scale the rule with text size. At 0.5dp the divider is already at the edge of visibility on low-density displays; it should hold its weight while type grows around it.

Divider Component

Architecture

Why the simplest component in the system still has a variant axis, and why Section Divider is built out of Divider rather than beside it.

Model

The Configuration Model #

A rule needs no configuration. An inset rule does — and that is the entire axis.

The Divider publishes one property, Padding, with five values. Four of them shift where the rule starts or stops; the fifth is None. Nothing else varies: weight, colour and height are fixed across every variant. That makes Divider the one component in Monocore where the variant axis is purely spatial.

The reason the inset lives on the component rather than the host is alignment. In a list with 16dp leading content, the rule has to start where the text starts, not where the row starts — otherwise it reads as a boundary around the avatar rather than between two rows. Putting that inset in the component means the value travels with the design system instead of being re-derived in every list.

Zero height is the contract. The Divider box is 0dp tall with the rule drawn on its top edge, so dropping one into an auto-layout stack changes nothing about the stack's rhythm. Every gap you see around a divider belongs to the host. A component that reserved its own vertical space would make list spacing depend on whether a divider happened to be present.
Structure

Figma Anatomy #

Both published components. Purple entries are slots, blue are bound text properties, and items marked optional are boolean-toggled per instance.

Divider105360-136054 · 5 variants
Divider (Padding · height 0 · fills container width) └─ Stroke (height 0, width 100% · 0.5dp rule on the top edge · Stroke/Divider)
Section Divider83796-188604 · 2 variants
Section Divider (Orientation · gap 8 · 375×28 horizontal, 82×205 vertical) ├─ Divider — leading rule (horizontal) / rotated Line (vertical, 1dp) ├─ Button → [slot] Slot (16×16 icon) + [text] Label — optional, ON by default ├─ Icon (12×12) — optional, off by default ├─ [text] Text — optional, off by default · iOS/Caption 1 └─ Divider — trailing rule (horizontal) / rotated Line (vertical, 1dp)
Section Divider consumes Divider, it does not re-draw it. The horizontal variant nests two real Divider instances, each set to fill the space left over by the centre element. That is why a change to the divider colour propagates to section breaks for free — and why the vertical variant, which does not use Divider, is the one that drifts.
Naming

Leading, Trailing, and What They Mean Here #

The variant names describe the edge that gets the inset, not the edge the rule reaches.

16-leading applies 16dp of padding on the leading edge, so the rule begins 16dp in and still runs to the far edge. 16-trailing does the mirror. Read literally the names are unambiguous, but they are easy to misread as “the rule leads by 16” — which would be the opposite. When implementing, map them to a directional inset (padding-inline-start / padding-inline-end) rather than to a physical left/right, so the component keeps working under RTL.

RTL is not handled by the component. The padding is authored as a physical inset in Figma. In code it must become logical, or every inset divider will point the wrong way in Arabic and Hebrew layouts.
Known issues

Published Debt #

IssueWhereEffect
Vertical Section Divider draws a 1dp rotated line instead of nesting DividerSection Divider · VerticalVertical rules are twice the weight of horizontal ones and will not follow future Divider changes
Button, Icon and Text are independent booleansSection Divider · both orientationsAll three can be on at once; there is no published constraint to one centre element
Button defaults to ONSection DividerThe plain rule-with-a-gap case requires switching a boolean off, making the least-decorated form the most work
No symmetric inset variantDividerBoth-ends insets get re-implemented per surface, which is exactly what the axis exists to prevent
The vertical weight mismatch is the one to fix first. It is the only issue here that is visible side by side — put a horizontal and a vertical section break on the same screen and the difference reads as a bug, not a choice.

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Figma page Empty List View; nodes: Empty state 106947:224790, Examples 108266:171243.

Community guidelines

Examples

Usage Examples #

The published examples place the component in three hosts, and its footer behaves differently in each.

HostPublished asNotes
Full screenScreen Template → Canvas slot, 402×794 above the tab barFooter sits above the Bottom sticky control
Full-screen sheetSheet → Content Slot, 402×718 under the drawer toolbarTitle centres in the reduced height automatically
Half sheet with keyboardSheet at 480dp with the keyboard raisedMain content compresses to 326dp — media, title and body still fit; the footer is the first thing to collide
The component owns the message, the host owns the height. Because Main content centres in the remainder, the empty state survives any host taller than roughly 400dp. Below that — a half sheet with a keyboard — drop the footer booleans rather than letting the buttons push the title off-canvas.
Accessibility

Accessibility #

  • The illustration is decorative. The Media slot's default artwork carries no information the title does not; expose it as decorative so it is not announced.
  • Reading order is the layout order. Title, description, link, then actions — keep the DOM/accessibility order matching the visual stack, especially when the custom title slot replaces the text title.
  • The deprecated description colour is the contrast risk. #6e6e6e on white is 4.9:1 — passing, but with no headroom, and it is not a live token so a theme change will not correct it.
  • One primary action. Three stacked full-width buttons force a screen-reader user through three equally-weighted choices on a screen whose entire message is “there is nothing here yet”. Prefer one, at most two.

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Figma page Filter; nodes: Horizontal filter button 116204:95563, Vertical filter button 108979:438444.

Examples

Usage Examples #

Both published examples put the pills in a horizontally-scrolling row directly under a search field or header.

Label People Files Channels Search — one applied filter (Primary, Active) beside unapplied Secondary pills
Unread Mentions Blocked Chat — a Secondary filter applied alongside a Danger filter
Filters live in a scrolling row, not a wrap. Both published examples keep every pill on one line and scroll horizontally. Wrapping to a second line turns a filter bar into a tag cloud and loses the reading order that makes the applied filter findable.
Accessibility

Accessibility #

  • Active must be announced, not just drawn. The pill is a toggle. Expose its applied state programmatically — a screen reader user has no access to the fill colour or the Semibold weight.
  • 32dp is under a 44dp target. Filter pills sit in a tight scrolling row, so undersized targets compound. Extend the hit area vertically; do not grow the pill.
  • Do not trust the 30% disabled state for contrast. Because Dissabled is opacity applied to the whole pill, the label fades with it. Disabled controls are exempt from contrast minimums, but this also means disabled state must never be the only signal that a filter is unavailable.
  • Danger is not conveyed by colour alone anywhere else. The Danger semantic differs from Secondary only in hue. If a destructive filter matters, pair it with an icon or wording — red on its own is not sufficient.

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboard, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Figma page Filter; node: Vertical filter button 108979:438444.

Examples

Usage Examples #

The published examples put the vertical filter in a chat header — a row of icon-over-label toggles above a message list.

Unread Chats Teams Files Apps Chat header — one applied filter beside four unapplied
Vertical is for a grid, horizontal is for a row. At 61 × 51 the vertical button is nearly square and reads as a tile; five of them fill a phone width. If your filters have labels longer than one short word, or you need more than about five, the horizontal pill is the right component.
Accessibility

Accessibility #

  • Active is conveyed by colour alone. Unlike the horizontal filter, there is no weight change between applied and unapplied. Until that is fixed at the source, the applied state must be exposed programmatically and should carry a non-colour cue in product.
  • 51dp tall, 61dp wide — the one filter that clears 44dp. Both dimensions pass, which makes this the better choice where mis-taps are costly.
  • The label clips rather than wraps. overflow: clip plus a solid 11dp line height means large text settings truncate silently. Treat the label as decorative reinforcement and put the real name in the accessible name.
  • The glyph is the only content in an icon-only instance. Turning Label off leaves nothing announceable — supply an accessible name explicitly.

Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. Notes

When to Use It #

Use Forward when the chiclet shows a message being passed on rather than replied to. The attribution carries a full date because a forwarded message has usually travelled further in time than a reply.

Reply and Forward differ by one icon. Every other value — padding, gap, quote bar, both type styles, both colours — is identical. Publishing them as two Layout values rather than one variant with an icon swap is a defensible call for discoverability, but it doubles the surface that has to stay in sync.

Accessibility

Accessibility #

  • The circular button is 28dp. It is the only control in the component and it is well under a 44dp target — the host must extend the hit area.
  • Recording state must be announced, not just tinted. The only difference between running and recording is a fill colour and a waveform. Neither reaches a screen reader; the state needs live-region text.
  • Timecode changes constantly. Do not put it in an assertive live region — a per-second announcement makes the rest of the screen unusable.

Chiclet Family

Chiclet Footer

The 28dp action row nested inside Chiclet / Layout = Base + actions. Published separately so the action pattern can be reused, and so the message chiclet does not have to publish an action variant per button count.

2 variants 1 axis 295 × 28dp Figma: Monocore-iOS · node 104574-8225
Reference

Both Patterns #

Pattern is the only axis. Group pairs two hugging buttons and keeps an overflow glyph on the trailing edge; Single stretches one button across the full width and drops the overflow entirely.

Pattern = Group

Pattern = Single — button fills the row, no overflow

Reference

Values #

PropertyGroupSingle
Row size295 × 28dp
Cross-axis alignmentCenterStart
ButtonsPrimary + Secondary, huggingOne, fills the row
Gap between buttons8dp Size/Small—
Overflow glyphMore Horizontal, 24×24dpNot published
Button styleSurface/RaisedTertiary fill, 0.5dp Stroke/ContainerRaised, radius 200 — the Button set's Outline accent · Small
Button padding8dp leading / 10dp trailing, gap 4dp, 16dp icon
LabeliOS/Button 2 — 13/18dp Medium, Text/Primary
Group centres its children, Single aligns them to the start. Both rows are 28dp tall and both buttons are 28dp, so the two settings happen to render identically today — but they will diverge the moment a button grows or the row gains padding. Set both to centre.
Both patterns use Outline accent, never Accent. The footer sits inside a chiclet that is already a card inside a message; a filled accent button at that depth competes with the message's own primary action. If a chiclet action needs to be the loudest thing on screen, the chiclet is the wrong container.

Chiclet Family

Overlay btn

The circular control that sits on top of media — dismiss on a file preview, play on a video. Two sizes, and a second pair for when there is no media to sit on.

4 variants 2 axes 24 / 48dp Figma: Monocore-iOS · node 106154-55456
Reference

All Four Variants #

Overlay switches the fill between a dark scrim and a plain surface with a border. Size switches padding and glyph, not the geometry of anything else.

Overlay = True · Size = Default
24×24dp
Overlay = True · Size = Large
48×48dp
Overlay = False · Size = Default
Overlay = False · Size = Large
Reference

Values #

PropertyOverlay = TrueOverlay = False
FillSurface/BtntAlphaPrimary — #292929 at 78%Surface/Primary — #ffffff
BorderNone1dp Stroke/Container — #e6e6e6
Radius999 — fully rounded
Padding — Default6dp, around a 12dp glyph box
Padding — Large10dp, around a 28dp glyph box
Default glyphDismiss — swapped for Play on Video chiclets
The scrim is what makes the glyph legible. Overlay = True exists because media is arbitrary — a white glyph on an unknown photograph has no guaranteed contrast, and the 78% scrim is what supplies it. Never reduce that opacity to show more of the image.
Default is 24dp; Large is 48dp. Only the Large variant clears a 44dp target on its own, and Default is the one used for dismiss on file previews — the smallest control in the family is the one that destroys the user's attachment. Extend the hit area or use Large.

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Figma page Buttons; nodes: Circular button 106947:205667.

Dev notes

How the annotations are read from Figma #

The page mirrors the Layout view one-to-one (same artboards, same sections, same blocks). For each component instance in a block, the bound variables are read from the instance itself: fills and strokes on the root give background and stroke, cornerRadius the radius, auto-layout frames give padding and gap, every visible text layer gives its colour and text style, and nested instances (icons, avatars, badges, and anything 160 px or smaller) give their size and colour. Each token is resolved for that instance (resolveForConsumer), so the raw value is what the instance actually renders in the file's current mode.

Reading the table. Element is the Figma layer the row describes (the component itself first, then its layers, texts and parts). Token is the Figma variable name; Value is its resolved raw value. A stroke listed as weight 0 is bound on the layer but not drawn. A colour listed at @ 0% is a bound colour with zero alpha, i.e. transparent. A dash means the property is set directly with no variable bound.

Figma page List; nodes: List types 106947:222146, Generic List 107060:96388.

Generic List is the family template. Timed list adds a timestamp, Accordion adds a chevron, Nested Accordion adds an inset, Grouped list adds a container. Fix a defect here first — the siblings inherit it.
Accessibility

Accessibility #

  • The row is one target; the trailing accessory is another. Both need separate accessible names, or the accessory folds into the row's single action.
  • Unread must be announced, not just bolded. The weight change and the 8dp dot are both visual-only; expose unread state programmatically.
  • Selected is colour-only. Surface/SubtleSelected against white is a 4%% luminance shift — announce selection, never rely on the tint.
  • Rows meet the 44dp floor only at Default. Verify the small/compact forms against the host's hit-area extension.

The timestamp answers “when”, the accessory answers “what next”. Keep the timestamp relative and short — it shares the first line with the label and steals truncation space from it.
Accessibility

Accessibility #

  • The row is one target; the trailing accessory is another. Both need separate accessible names, or the accessory folds into the row's single action.
  • Unread must be announced, not just bolded. The weight change and the 8dp dot are both visual-only; expose unread state programmatically.
  • Selected is colour-only. Surface/SubtleSelected against white is a 4%% luminance shift — announce selection, never rely on the tint.
  • Rows meet the 44dp floor only at Default. Verify the small/compact forms against the host's hit-area extension.

Also announce the timestamp as part of the row's name (“Priya Raman, 9:41, unread”) — a trailing text node read separately loses its subject.
